1.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
1.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between on-the-job and off-the-job training.
ans: On-the-job: training at the workplace while doing the job (e.g. mentoring) (2).
Off-the-job: training away from the normal workplace (e.g. college course, external provider) (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of off-the-job training.
ans: Access to specialist expertise/qualifications; fewer workplace distractions; broader skills. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a seasonal business (e.g. an ice-cream maker) often has low capacity utilisation for part of the year.
ans: Demand is concentrated in certain months, leaving capacity idle off-season -> high unit costs then. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way such a business could raise off-season capacity utilisation.
ans: Produce complementary counter-seasonal products, promotions, export to other hemispheres, subcontract capacity. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two selection methods a business could use.
ans: Any two: interviews, application forms/CV screening, references, aptitude/psychometric testing, assessment centres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of relying only on interviews to select staff.
ans: Subjective/prone to bias; good interviewees may be poor performers; does not test practical skills; first-impression effect. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘motivation’.
ans: The internal drive/desire (1) that causes people to act to achieve a goal, e.g. to work towards business objectives (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why motivating employees is important to a business.
ans: Higher productivity/quality and effort; lower absenteeism and turnover.
Better customer service, more ideas/initiative, easier change.
Up to 5 for developed explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the main idea of Taylor’s theory of motivation.
ans: Scientific management: workers are motivated mainly by money (1); find the most efficient way to work and pay by results/piece rate (1) with close control/division of labour (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one criticism of Taylor’s approach to motivation.
ans: Ignores social/psychological needs; treats workers as machines; can lower morale/creativity. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘maximum capacity’.
ans: The greatest output a business can produce with its existing resources in a given period (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how investing in new technology could raise both capacity and productivity.
ans: More/faster machines raise maximum output (capacity) and output per worker (productivity).
Lowers unit costs and lead times, improving competitiveness; but high cost and possible job losses.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States link, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three main methods of market segmentation.
ans: Geographic (1), demographic (1) and psychographic (1) (accept behavioural).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse two benefits to a business of segmenting its market.
ans: Targets marketing more precisely -> higher response/lower waste.
Tailors product/price to segment needs -> higher satisfaction and possibly premium prices.
Identifies gaps/new segments; improves customer retention.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two benefits analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies benefits, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a consumer market and an industrial market.
ans: Consumer (B2C): goods/services sold to households for personal use (2).
Industrial (B2B): goods/services sold to other businesses for use in production (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way marketing differs between B2C and B2B.
ans: B2B: fewer, larger buyers, relationship/technical selling, negotiated prices; B2C: mass promotion, branding, emotional appeal. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between trade receivables and trade payables.
ans: Trade receivables: money owed to the business by credit customers (2).
Trade payables: money the business owes to its suppliers (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a business could reduce its trade receivables.
ans: Tighter credit terms, prompt-payment discounts, debt factoring, credit checks/chasing. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘business ethics’.
ans: Moral principles/values (1) that guide how a business behaves and makes decisions (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how ethical considerations might influence a clothing firm’s objectives.
ans: May adopt objectives on fair wages/no child labour in the supply chain.
Sustainable materials/reduced waste objectives.
May sacrifice some short-term profit for long-term reputation/legality.
Up to 5 for applied explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a business could use the Boston Matrix to make marketing decisions.
ans: Invest in stars (high growth, high share) to become future cash cows.
Use cash-cow revenue to fund stars/question marks; decide which question marks to back or drop.
Divest dogs; aim for a balanced portfolio.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of the product life cycle model for making marketing decisions.
ans: For: guides mix changes, extension strategies and portfolio planning; simple/widely used.
Against: hard to know the current stage; not all products follow the curve (fads, classics); length of stages varies; can become self-fulfilling if withdrawal is premature.
Judgement: a useful planning tool if used flexibly alongside data, not a precise predictor. Depends on product/market.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the effects on a business of operating below its maximum capacity.
ans: High fixed cost per unit -> higher average cost, lower profit/competitiveness.
Idle resources, possible low morale; but spare capacity allows flexibility/new orders and maintenance.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis both effects.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the best way for a business to improve low capacity utilisation.
ans: Options: raise demand (marketing/price), rationalise (cut capacity), subcontract for others, diversify.
Trade-offs: boosting demand keeps capacity but risks unsold stock; rationalising cuts cost but limits future growth and causes redundancies.
Judgement: depends on whether low demand is temporary or permanent and on finance; if temporary, boost demand/subcontract; if permanent, rationalise. Context-dependent.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse why a growing market share can benefit a business.
ans: Higher sales/revenue and economies of scale lowering unit costs.
Greater market power/brand strength, bargaining power with suppliers/retailers.
Can support price leadership and deter entrants.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Understanding customers is more important than beating competitors.’ Evaluate this view for a marketing manager.
ans: For customers: needs-led (market orientation) drives loyalty, retention and the right products; source of long-term success.
For competitors: must monitor rivals to remain competitive on price/features and defend share.
Judgement: both matter and interlink; deep customer understanding usually the foundation, but ignoring competitors is dangerous. Depends on market rivalry.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how the form of business ownership affects the sources of finance available.
ans: Sole trader/partnership: limited to owners’ funds, loans, trade credit, retained profit – no share issue.
Ltd: can sell shares privately; plc: can raise large equity on the stock market.
Limited liability and track record affect lender/investor willingness.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the factors a business should consider when choosing a source of finance.
ans: Cost (interest/dividends/fees), flexibility, need to retain control, use (short vs long term), level of existing debt (gearing), risk.
Trade-offs: debt keeps control but adds fixed cost/risk; equity avoids repayment but dilutes control.
Judgement: most important factor depends on purpose, ownership and financial position; matching source to need is key.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘focus group’.
ans: A small group of consumers led in discussion by a researcher (1) to gather qualitative opinions about a product/idea (1).

parts.text: Identify whether the survey and focus groups are primary or secondary research, and justify your answer.
ans: Primary research (1) – first-hand data collected by FreshFizz for this specific launch (2).

parts.text: Using Table 1, calculate how many of the 500 respondents said they would try the drink.
ans: =64% × 500 = 320 respondents
2 method + 1 answer (320).

parts.text: Explain one reason the directors are right to question the reliability of the survey.
ans: The sample was only existing FreshFizz website visitors -> self-selected/biased towards fans, not the whole target market.
Results may overstate interest; sample of 500 may be small for a national launch.
1–2 + development.

parts.text: Analyse how FreshFizz could use the research findings to develop a USP for the drink.
ans: Focus groups value taste and a ‘natural’ image -> build USP around natural ingredients/great taste.
Only 41% will pay a premium, so the USP should not rely solely on price positioning.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Uses data to shape a USP.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies a USP, limited use of data.

parts.text: Recommend how FreshFizz should position the new drink, using the research. Justify your recommendation and note the limitations of the data.
ans: #Positioning options
Premium ‘natural, great-tasting’ low-sugar drink for 18–34s vs mass low-price drink.
#Use of data
High trial interest (64%) and weekly purchase (72%) support a mainstream launch; taste (58%) and natural image key; only 41% pay premium -> cautious on premium pricing.
#Limitations
Biased sample (website visitors) may overstate demand -> further, representative research advised before large investment.
#Judgement
Supported recommendation, e.g. position on taste + natural image at a competitive (not high-premium) price, targeting 18–34s, but validate with wider research first.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses data, justified recommendation with awareness of reliability.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

2.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
2.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A business has an opening cash balance of $12,000, receipts of $34,000 and payments of $41,000 in a month. Calculate the closing balance.
ans: 2 method + 1 answer ($5,000).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way this business could improve its cash flow.
ans: Delay payments/negotiate credit, chase receivables, cut costs, arrange overdraft, delay capital spending, sale and leaseback. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘share capital’.
ans: Finance raised by selling shares in a company (1) to shareholders who become part-owners (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one drawback of raising finance by issuing more shares.
ans: Dilutes ownership/control and profits (dividends) among more shareholders; risk of takeover. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘unfair dismissal’.
ans: Ending employment without a fair/legal reason (1) or without following a fair procedure (1), giving the employee grounds to claim (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why following a fair dismissal procedure matters to a business.
ans: Avoids legal claims/compensation and reputational damage; maintains morale/fairness. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘market research’.
ans: The systematic gathering and analysis of data (1) about customers, competitors and the market to inform marketing decisions (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two purposes of conducting market research.
ans: Identify customer needs/wants and profiles.
Assess market size, growth and competitors; reduce risk of a new launch.
Test the marketing mix (price/product/promotion).
#Marks
Up to 3 per purpose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between digital and physical distribution channels.
ans: Physical: goods reach customers through wholesalers/retailers/physical stores (2).
Digital: products/services delivered or sold online (e-commerce, downloads/streaming) (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit to a manufacturer of selling directly to consumers online.
ans: Higher margins (no intermediary), direct customer data/relationship, control of brand. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the stages of business decision-making.
ans: Set objectives -> gather data/information -> analyse options -> make decision -> implement -> review/evaluate against objectives (any logical sequence, 3 marks).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse the role of objectives in the decision-making process.
ans: Objectives provide the criteria against which options are judged.
They guide data collection and focus analysis on relevant factors.
They provide the benchmark for the review/evaluation stage.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of objectives’ role at each stage.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States role, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘corporate social responsibility (CSR)’.
ans: A business acting ethically and considering its impact on society and the environment (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse one benefit and one cost of CSR to a business.
ans: Benefit: reputation/loyalty, staff motivation, differentiation.
Cost: higher operating costs may reduce short-term profit.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Both sides analysed.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘budget’.
ans: A financial plan for a future period (1) setting out expected income and/or expenditure/targets (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two purposes of budgeting for a business.
ans: Planning – sets financial targets and allocates resources.
Control/monitoring – compares actual with budget (variance analysis).
Motivation and coordination of departments.
#Marks
Up to 3 per purpose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘diversity’ in the workplace.
ans: Employing people from a wide range of backgrounds – e.g. gender, age, ethnicity, ability (1) – and valuing their differences (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how a diverse and inclusive workforce can benefit a business.
ans: Wider range of ideas/creativity and better understanding of diverse customers.
Larger talent pool, improved reputation, compliance with equality law.
Higher morale/retention where staff feel valued.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of benefits.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States benefits, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘stakeholder conflict’.
ans: A situation where the aims of different stakeholder groups clash (1) so satisfying one group harms another (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how conflict might arise between shareholders and employees when a business tries to cut costs.
ans: Shareholders want higher profit/dividends -> pressure to cut wages or jobs.
Employees want secure jobs and good pay -> resist redundancies/pay freezes.
Cost-cutting to satisfy shareholders can lower morale, productivity and industrial relations.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of the conflict.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States conflict, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how accurate cost information helps a business make better decisions.
ans: Informs pricing (cover costs + margin), product mix and make-or-buy/special orders.
Enables cost control, budgeting and profit calculation.
Poor cost data -> mispricing/loss-making decisions.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether contribution costing is more useful than full costing for decision-making.
ans: For contribution: avoids arbitrary overhead allocation, ideal for short-term/special-order/make-or-buy and break-even decisions.
Against: ignores fixed costs which must be covered long-term; risk of under-pricing; full costing better for long-run pricing and product profitability.
Judgement: contribution is better for short-term marginal decisions with spare capacity; full costing for long-term pricing. Depends on the decision. Use both.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how the factors of production are used to add value in a manufacturing business.
ans: Land/raw materials transformed via labour and capital (machinery) organised by enterprise.
Each stage of the transformation raises worth: raw input -> work-in-progress -> finished good.
Value added = selling price minus bought-in inputs; efficient use of factors raises it.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis of the transformation/value-adding process.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some analysis.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the importance of a business plan to an entrepreneur seeking external finance.
ans: For: evidences viability, forecasts repayment ability, reduces perceived lender risk, may be a condition of a loan/grant.
Against: forecasts are only estimates and may be over-optimistic; lenders also weigh collateral, credit history and the entrepreneur’s track record; a plan does not guarantee funding or success.
Judgement: important but not sufficient on its own; value depends on realism of the plan and the type of finance sought.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Supported judgement with balanced argument and context.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two-sided, limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how changes in supply and demand could affect the price and sales of coffee for a cafe chain.
ans: A poor harvest cuts supply of beans -> input prices rise -> higher costs/prices.
A health trend or rising incomes raises demand -> higher prices/sales.
The chain must respond via pricing/menu decisions.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis using demand/supply.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the importance of setting SMART marketing objectives for a business launching a new product.
ans: For: focus, coordination, measurement, motivation, benchmark to judge the launch.
Against: uncertain new markets make realistic targets hard; rigid objectives may not adapt; success also depends on execution and rivals.
Judgement: valuable for control but must be flexible/reviewed; important yet not sufficient on its own.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how translating objectives into budgets and targets can help a business monitor performance.
ans: Budgets convert objectives into financial plans for departments.
Actual results compared with budget reveal variances/problems early.
Targets give individuals clear, measurable goals to be reviewed.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Ethical behaviour and profitability cannot go together.’ Evaluate this statement.
ans: For: ethics raise costs (fair wages, sustainable inputs), may reduce short-term profit or competitiveness on price.
Against: ethics attract customers/staff, avoid fines/scandal, build long-term loyalty and can be a USP; unethical conduct risks reputational and legal disaster.
Judgement: often a short-term cost but long-term benefit; depends on market and how ethics are managed. Not mutually exclusive.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘capacity utilisation’.
ans: The percentage of maximum possible output currently being used (2).

parts.text: Using Table 1, calculate Orion’s current capacity utilisation.
ans: 2 method + 1 answer (97%).

parts.text: Identify two problems shown in the case of operating near full capacity.
ans: Any two: rising overtime cost ($310k); quality complaints; late deliveries ($95k penalties); overworked staff/machines.

parts.text: Using Table 1, estimate the annual saving if all 58,200 bikes used outsourced frames.
ans: 2 method + 1 answer (≈$1.05m).

parts.text: Analyse the case for and against outsourcing frame production, using the data.
ans: For: large saving (≈$1.05m/yr), adds capacity without $2.5m investment, flexible if boom fades.
Against: quality complaints already an issue – less control overseas; long lead times worsen late-delivery penalties ($95k); reliance/ethical/reputation risk.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Balanced analysis using figures.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.text: Recommend which option Orion should choose to deal with the capacity problem. Justify your recommendation using the case and data.
ans: #Weigh options

New line: solves capacity long-term and quality, but $2.5m risk if the boom fades (utilisation was only 62% in 2023). Outsourcing: big saving/flexible but control/lead-time risk. Overtime: quick but costly ($310k) and hurting quality/delivery.
#Judgement

Supported recommendation, e.g. because the boom may be temporary, favour outsourcing and/or continued overtime for flexibility now, delaying the $2.5m investment until demand proves sustained; or invest if confident demand is permanent. Use utilisation trend (62%->97%) to justify caution.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses data, justified recommendation aware of demand uncertainty.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

3.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
3.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘buffer inventory’.
ans: A minimum level of inventory held as a safety margin (1) to cover unexpected demand or delivery delays (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one cost of holding too much inventory.
ans: Storage, insurance, obsolescence/spoilage, and cash tied up (opportunity cost) that could be used elsewhere. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between the tangible and intangible attributes of a product.
ans: Tangible: physical/measurable features – size, materials, performance (2).
Intangible: image, brand, reputation, after-sales service (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why intangible attributes can be important for a car manufacturer.
ans: Brand image/status and reliability reputation influence purchase and allow premium pricing. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘penetration pricing’.
ans: Setting a low initial price to enter a market/gain market share quickly (1), then possibly raising it later (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain a situation where penetration pricing would be appropriate.
ans: A new product entering a competitive mass market with price-sensitive buyers, aiming for volume/market share. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘work in progress’.
ans: Partly finished goods that are still being processed (1) – between raw materials and finished output (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a business could reduce the amount of cash tied up in inventory.
ans: Adopt JIT/lower buffer, improve forecasting, faster stock turnover, better supplier links. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘economic order quantity’ (in simple terms).
ans: The order size that minimises total inventory costs (1) – balancing ordering costs against holding costs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse the trade-off between ordering in large batches and ordering little and often.
ans: Large batches: bulk discounts, fewer orders, but high holding cost and cash tied up/obsolescence risk.
Small frequent orders (JIT): low holding cost but higher ordering/delivery cost and stock-out risk.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of the trade-off.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States trade-off, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between capital-intensive and labour-intensive operations.
ans: Capital-intensive: production relies mainly on machinery/technology (2).
Labour-intensive: production relies mainly on human effort/workers (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit of capital-intensive production.
ans: Consistent quality, high output/low unit cost at volume, works continuously, fewer labour disputes. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the formula for capacity utilisation.
ans: (Current output / maximum possible output) × 100 (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse two problems of operating at very low capacity utilisation.
ans: Fixed costs spread over few units -> high unit cost/low profit.
Idle machinery/labour, low morale, sign of low demand.
Uncompetitive pricing.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two problems analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies problems, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘sustainability’ in operations.
ans: Meeting present needs (1) without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs (1) – minimising environmental/resource damage in production (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse one benefit and one cost to a business of making operations more sustainable.
ans: Benefit: lower long-term costs (energy/waste), better reputation, meets regulation/customer demand.
Cost: high upfront investment (new equipment/processes), possible higher short-term unit cost.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Both sides analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies a benefit/cost, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between JIT and JIC (Just in Case).
ans: JIT: minimal stock, delivered as needed – low holding cost but vulnerable to disruption (2).
JIC: holds buffer stock ‘just in case’ – secure supply but higher holding costs (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one situation where JIC is more appropriate than JIT.
ans: Unreliable supply chains, volatile demand, or where stock-outs are very costly (e.g. hospitals). 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘contribution per unit’.
ans: Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A product sells for $30, variable cost $18, fixed costs $48,000. Calculate the break-even output.
ans: =Contribution = 30 − 18 = $12
=Break-even = 48,000 / 12 = 4,000 units

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the factors a business should consider when choosing a channel of distribution.
ans: Nature of product (perishable, technical, bulky), target market and their buying habits.
Cost/margin, control of brand, reach/coverage, competitors’ channels.
Digital capability and speed.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the view that digital promotion has made traditional advertising unnecessary.
ans: For digital: cheaper, targeted, measurable, interactive, growing reach, essential for e-commerce.
Against: traditional (TV, print, outdoor) still reaches mass/older audiences, builds brand, high trust; ad-blocking/fraud online; best mix depends on audience.
Judgement: digital is dominant and growing but not a total replacement; an integrated mix is usually best. Depends on target market and budget.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how the reliability of market research data affects the quality of business decisions.
ans: Unreliable data (small/biased sample, leading questions) -> wrong conclusions and poor decisions.
Reliable data improves forecasting, targeting and confidence.
Sample size/method and source all matter.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the importance of a unique selling point to the success of a product.
ans: For: differentiation, premium pricing, loyalty, easier promotion, defence against competition.
Against: USPs can be copied; price, place, service and brand also matter; some markets compete mainly on price/convenience.
Judgement: important in crowded/differentiated markets but not sufficient alone; must be supported by the whole mix. Depends on market.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse why market research is important before launching a new product.
ans: Tests whether demand exists and identifies target customers/needs -> reduces failure risk.
Informs the marketing mix (price point, features, channels, message).
Estimates market size/competition to forecast sales/finance.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether primary research is always better than secondary research for a small business.
ans: Primary: specific, current, exclusive, tailored; but costly, slow and needs expertise.
Secondary: cheap, quick, good for market size/trends; but may be out of date, general or available to rivals.
Judgement: for a small budget, start with cheap secondary research then targeted primary; primary not always better – depends on cost, time and the decision.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the impact of outsourcing on a business and its stakeholders.
ans: Business: lower costs, flexibility, focus on core; but less control and reliance on suppliers.
Employees: possible job losses/insecurity; customers: quality may rise or fall; suppliers gain work.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis across the business/stakeholders.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether a business should outsource a key part of its production to a lower-cost country.
ans: For: significant cost savings, capacity/expertise, competitiveness.
Against: quality/control risk, long lead times/supply disruption, communication/culture, ethical/reputation concerns, job losses at home.
Judgement: depends on whether it is core/differentiating, cost savings vs risks, and reliability; may outsource non-core, keep core in-house. Context-dependent.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘induction training’.
ans: Training given to new employees when they join (1) to introduce them to the business, their role, colleagues and procedures (1).

parts.text: Using Table 1, calculate Meridian’s labour turnover rate for the year.
ans: =Labour turnover = (375 / 1,250) × 100 = 30%
2 method + 1 answer (30%).

parts.text: Using Table 1, estimate the annual cost to Meridian of replacing the staff who left.
ans: =375 leavers × $1,600 = $600,000 per year
2 method + 1 answer.

parts.text: Explain two likely causes of Meridian’s high labour turnover, using the case.
ans: Poor induction (46% leave within 3 months) – staff feel unprepared/unsupported.
Low pay relative to the market; rushed, weak selection producing poor job fit.
1–2 per cause with application.

parts.text: Analyse how introducing structured selection and improved induction could benefit Meridian.
ans: Better job fit -> fewer early leavers -> lower turnover and recruitment cost ($600k).
Induction raises confidence, productivity and morale, improving guest service/quality.
Supports the planned expansion by building a stable, capable workforce.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis linking the changes to case problems/costs.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some analysis.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.text: The board must decide whether to adopt the HR director’s three proposals before expanding. Recommend what Meridian should do. Justify your answer.
ans: #For adopting now
Cuts the 30% turnover and $600k cost, builds capability for six new hotels, improves guest experience/reputation.
#Against / concerns
Slower and costlier short term; rooms need staffing immediately; managers resist.
#Judgement

Supported recommendation, e.g. phase in the workforce plan and induction before expansion to avoid repeating the turnover problem at a larger scale; prioritise the cheapest high-impact change (induction) first.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses data, justified recommendation.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

4.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
4.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between cost-based pricing and competitive pricing.
ans: Cost-based: price set by adding a mark-up to unit cost (2).
Competitive: price set in line with/relative to competitors’ prices (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of cost-based pricing.
ans: Ignores demand/what customers will pay and competitors; may price too high (lose sales) or too low (lose profit). 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘dynamic pricing’.
ans: Adjusting prices in real time (1) in response to demand, timing or customer data (1), e.g. airline/ride-hailing prices (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one risk of using dynamic pricing.
ans: Customers may feel exploited/unfair -> reputation damage; complexity; needs data/systems. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘market growth’.
ans: The increase in the total size/sales of a market over a period (1), usually shown as a percentage change (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse the implications for a business of operating in a rapidly growing market.
ans: Opportunity for higher sales/economies of scale and new customers.
But attracts new competitors; needs investment/capacity; risk of overtrading.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of implications.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States implications, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘batch production’.
ans: Producing groups (batches) of identical products (1) that move through each stage together before switching to the next product (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one problem of changing from batch to flow production.
ans: High investment in line/equipment, retraining, downtime during changeover, loss of flexibility, redundancy costs. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of branding in promotion.
ans: Builds recognition, trust and loyalty; differentiates; supports premium pricing and repeat purchase. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the role of packaging in promotion.
ans: Attracts attention, communicates brand/information, protects product, can be a USP/differentiator. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a multinational business and a national business.
ans: National: operates (produces/sells) within one country only (2).
Multinational: has production/operating facilities in more than one country, not merely exporting (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason a business may become multinational.
ans: Access to larger markets/sales growth; lower production costs (cheaper labour/materials); avoid tariffs/trade barriers; spread risk. 1 mark reason + 2 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between contribution and profit.
ans: Contribution = sales revenue minus total variable costs (covers fixed costs first).
Profit = total contribution minus fixed costs; profit only arises once fixed costs are covered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one use of contribution costing.
ans: Break-even analysis, special-order/make-or-buy decisions, product profitability, pricing. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘outsourcing’.
ans: Contracting out a business activity/process to an external provider (1) rather than doing it in-house (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse one benefit and one drawback of outsourcing production.
ans: Benefit: lower costs, access to specialist expertise/capacity, flexibility, focus on core activities.
Drawback: less control over quality/timing, reliance on supplier, possible reputation/ethical risk, communication issues.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Both sides analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies a benefit/drawback, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘capacity utilisation’.
ans: The proportion of a business’s maximum possible output that is currently being used (1), expressed as a percentage (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A factory with maximum output of 5,000 units produces 3,750. Calculate its capacity utilisation.
ans: =Capacity utilisation = (3,750 / 5,000) × 100 = 75%
2 method + 1 answer (75%).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘business plan’.
ans: A written document (1) setting out a business idea, its objectives and how they will be achieved – including marketing, operations and financial forecasts (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits of writing a business plan before starting up.
ans: Helps secure finance: lenders/investors assess viability from forecasts.
Clarifies objectives and identifies risks/resource needs before money is committed.
Acts as a benchmark to monitor performance against once trading.
#Marks
Up to 3 marks per benefit (identification + development).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the management roles identified by Mintzberg.
ans: Interpersonal (figurehead, leader, liaison).
Informational (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson).
Decisional (entrepreneur, disturbance-handler, resource allocator, negotiator).
Shows management is broader than Fayol’s functions.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of the role categories.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Lists roles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘A paternalistic style is the most suitable for managing a young, inexperienced workforce.’ Evaluate.
ans: For: guidance/support, welfare focus, clear direction suits inexperienced staff and can build loyalty.
Against: can be seen as controlling/patronising, limits development of initiative; democratic or coaching styles may develop staff faster; depends on individuals.
Judgement: paternalistic can suit early stages but should evolve as staff gain experience; depends on context.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the factors that determine the re-order level and re-order quantity a business should set.
ans: Lead time and its reliability; rate of usage/demand and its variability.
Cost of holding vs ordering; storage capacity; supplier discounts and reliability.
Risk/cost of a stock-out.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘A JIC (Just in Case) approach is safer and therefore always better than JIT.’ Evaluate.
ans: For JIC: security of supply, no stock-outs, copes with demand spikes and unreliable suppliers.
Against: high holding costs, cash tied up, obsolescence/waste; JIT is cheaper and leaner where supply is reliable.
Judgement: ‘safer’ but not always ‘better’ – depends on cost of holding vs cost of disruption; many firms use a hybrid. Context-dependent.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a manager’s choice of leadership style could affect employee motivation.
ans: Autocratic: quick decisions but may demotivate/limit initiative.
Democratic/paternalistic: involvement raises morale and ideas but is slower.
Laissez-faire: suits skilled/creative staff but risks lack of direction.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis linking styles to motivation.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the view that there is one best management style for all situations.
ans: For one style: consistency, clarity, e.g. democratic often praised for motivation.
Against: best style depends on task urgency, staff skill/motivation, culture, and the manager – a contingency view; autocratic suits crises, laissez-faire suits experts.
Judgement: no single best style; effective managers adapt (situational leadership).
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the factors a business should consider when choosing between labour-intensive and capital-intensive production.
ans: Scale/volume of output and demand stability; capital suits high, steady volumes.
Cost/availability of labour vs capital; product (bespoke favours labour).
Finance available; need for flexibility vs consistency; skills.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of several factors.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether investing to improve productivity is always the best way to raise competitiveness.
ans: For: lower unit costs, higher output, better prices/margins, funds further investment.
Against: high cost/risk, may cut jobs/morale, quality or differentiation may matter more than cost; competitiveness also from branding, service, innovation.
Judgement: depends on the basis of competition (cost vs differentiation) and finance; productivity matters but is not always the best route.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘collective bargaining’.
ans: Negotiation of pay/conditions between an employer and a trade union representing a group of workers (2).

parts.text: Identify two signs from Table 1 that morale at Novak is falling.
ans: Any two: labour turnover up 9%->17%; absenteeism up 4%->9%; output per worker down 1,120->990; 11 days lost to disputes (from 0).

parts.text: Explain how the way management introduced the new shift system may have worsened workforce relations.
ans: Imposed without consultation -> workers feel undervalued/ignored, breeding resentment and the strike ballot.
Lack of communication damages trust and cooperation.
1–2 link + 2 development.

parts.text: Analyse how improved training and multi-skilling could help Novak.
ans: Raises productivity/quality (reversing the fall in output per worker) and flexibility to cover shifts.
Improves morale/retention, reducing turnover and absenteeism.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Analysed with case data.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies benefits, limited application.

parts.text: Analyse how better cooperation with the trade union could benefit Novak.
ans: Consultation gives a channel to resolve the shift dispute, avoiding costly strikes (11 days lost).
Involving workers raises morale and buy-in to change, improving productivity.
Reduces turnover of experienced staff/supervisors and improves reputation.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis using the case.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.text: The finance director argues Novak ‘cannot afford’ the proposed package. Evaluate whether Novak should implement the operations director’s proposals. Justify your answer.
ans: #For implementing
Addresses root causes; likely to cut turnover/absence, restore output and avoid strike costs; long-term competitiveness and reputation.
#Against / concerns
Upfront cost while profits fall; benefits take time and are uncertain; risk of raising expectations.
#Judgement

Supported recommendation, e.g. phase in the lowest-cost, highest-impact elements first (consultation and communication cost little) and fund welfare/training from the productivity gains; not acting risks escalating disputes and falling output.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses data, justified recommendation.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

5.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
5.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the main finding of Mayo’s Hawthorne studies.
ans: Workers are motivated by social factors/group belonging and attention (1); productivity rose when workers felt valued/consulted (1) – the human relations school (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a business could apply Mayo’s findings.
ans: Teamworking, involving/consulting staff, showing interest/recognition. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons a business needs finance.
ans: Any two: to start up, to fund day-to-day operations/working capital, to grow/expand, to survive a shortfall, to invest in assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between a short-term and a long-term need for finance.
ans: Short-term: to fund day-to-day operations/working capital (e.g. wages, stock) – met by overdraft/trade credit.
Long-term: to fund non-current assets/expansion (e.g. premises, machinery) – met by loans/share capital.
Up to 5 for developed distinction with examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘product life cycle’.
ans: The stages a product passes through over time – development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline (1) – shown by sales over time (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two extension strategies a business could use to prolong the maturity stage.
ans: New uses/markets; restyling or new features/variants.
New packaging, increased promotion, price changes, targeting new segments.
#Marks
Up to 3 per strategy (identification + development).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘employee development’.
ans: Longer-term growth of employees’ skills, knowledge and careers (1) beyond immediate job training (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how employee development can encourage intrapreneurship.
ans: Builds skills/confidence and empowerment so staff generate and pursue new ideas within the firm. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘unlimited liability’.
ans: The owner(s) are personally responsible for all business debts (1); personal assets can be used to settle them (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why unlimited liability may discourage a sole trader from expanding.
ans: Expansion often requires borrowing/greater risk; losses could cost the owner personal assets (home, savings).
This deters risk-taking and limits access to external equity (cannot sell shares).
Fear of personal ruin may cap the scale the owner is willing to reach.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis linking unlimited liability to reluctance to grow.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States the idea with limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between quantitative and qualitative data.
ans: Quantitative: numerical data that can be measured/statistically analysed (2).
Qualitative: opinions/attitudes/reasons, descriptive and harder to measure (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a business might use both types of data.
ans: Quantitative shows how many/how much; qualitative explains why – together give fuller insight. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between full costing and contribution costing.
ans: Full (absorption) costing: allocates all costs, including a share of overheads, to each product (2).
Contribution costing: charges only variable costs to products; fixed costs treated as a period cost (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of full costing.
ans: Overhead allocation is often arbitrary, which can distort product costs/decisions. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between an internal and an external stakeholder.
ans: Internal: within the business – owners, managers, employees (2).
External: outside but affected by/interested in it – customers, suppliers, government, local community (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two rights of employees as stakeholders.
ans: Any: fair pay, safe working conditions, contract/legal protection, consultation, non-discrimination. 1 each + 1 for a developed example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘internal recruitment’.
ans: Filling a vacancy with an existing employee of the business (1) rather than an outsider (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse two advantages of internal recruitment over external recruitment.
ans: Cheaper/faster; candidate is a known quantity (lower selection risk).
Motivates staff (promotion prospects), retains firm-specific knowledge, shorter induction.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two advantages analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies advantages, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two methods of primary research.
ans: Any two: questionnaires/surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation, test marketing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse one limitation of using questionnaires.
ans: Risk of biased/leading questions or dishonest answers.
Low response rates and unrepresentative samples reduce reliability.
Costly/time-consuming to design and analyse well.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of a limitation.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States limitation, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse why involving staff in the budgeting process can benefit a business.
ans: Uses front-line knowledge -> more accurate/realistic budgets.
Increases ownership, motivation and commitment to targets.
Improves communication and coordination.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of budgets as a control tool in a fast-changing market.
ans: For: still provide targets, resource allocation and early warning via variances; flexible/rolling budgets adapt.
Against: rapid change makes fixed budgets quickly outdated/inaccurate; can constrain responsiveness; time-consuming to revise.
Judgement: useful if flexible/regularly updated (rolling/flexible budgets); rigid annual budgets are of limited use in volatile markets.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how improving productivity could affect a business’s costs and competitiveness.
ans: Higher output per worker/machine -> lower unit costs.
Enables lower prices or higher margins and faster delivery.
Improves competitiveness; but investment/training cost and possible job cuts.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether a business should always prioritise the interests of its shareholders over other stakeholders.
ans: For: owners risk capital; profit funds survival/investment.
Against: ignoring employees, customers, community harms reputation, morale and long-term value; stakeholder balance often best serves shareholders long-term.
Judgement: depends on time horizon; balancing stakeholders usually maximises long-run shareholder value.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the role of the entrepreneur in creating and starting up a business.
ans: Spots an opportunity/gap and develops the business idea (innovation).
Organises/combines the factors of production and writes the business plan.
Raises finance and bears the financial risk of the venture.
Makes key start-up decisions (location, product, pricing) and provides leadership.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Well-developed analysis of several roles, applied and logically sequenced.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some analysis of the entrepreneur’s roles.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identifies roles with little development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘The single most important quality for entrepreneurial success is a willingness to take risks.’ Evaluate this view.
ans: For: risk-taking is essential to commit resources under uncertainty; without it no venture begins.
Against: determination, innovation, financial literacy, leadership and effective market research may matter more; reckless risk-taking causes failure.
It depends on the industry, the stage of the business and the individual; calculated (not blind) risk-taking is what matters.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced evaluation, supported judgement on the relative importance of qualities, with context.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced discussion, some judgement.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two-sided but limited development / no real judgement.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided or assertion only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a cash flow forecast can help a business avoid a liquidity crisis.
ans: Predicts months of negative closing balance in advance -> arrange finance/overdraft early.
Guides timing of spending, credit terms and stock purchases.
Provides an early-warning control tool; but only as accurate as its assumptions.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of break-even analysis to a small manufacturer.
ans: For: simple, shows break-even output, margin of safety and effect of price/cost changes; aids planning and finance applications.
Against: assumes constant price/costs and that all output is sold; ignores discounts/economies of scale; data may be inaccurate; static in a changing market.
Judgement: a useful quick planning/decision tool if assumptions are understood; should be combined with realistic forecasts, not relied on alone.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘brand’.
ans: A name/design/symbol that identifies a product and differentiates it from competitors (2).

parts.text: Calculate the contribution per garment.
ans: =Contribution = 60 − 27 = $33 per garment

parts.text: Using the data, calculate Zephyr’s break-even output (garments per year).
ans: =Break-even = fixed costs / contribution = 5,280,000 / 33 = 160,000 garments per year
2 method + 1 answer (160,000).

parts.text: Explain one reason Zephyr should protect its premium brand during expansion.
ans: The premium brand supports high price/margin (contribution $33) and loyalty; scaling up carelessly could dilute quality/image and lose the price premium.
1–2 + development.

parts.text: Analyse how Zephyr should finance the expansion, given the directors’ concerns.
ans: Low existing debt and 11% margin mean a bank loan is affordable and keeps control (no dilution).
Retained earnings could part-fund it, protecting cash; avoid over-gearing to satisfy the cautious finance director.
Consider matching long-term finance (loan) to long-life assets (factory).
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis using data/constraints.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.text: Recommend how Zephyr should manage the expansion across marketing, operations and finance to protect its brand and grow successfully. Justify your answer.
ans: #Marketing
Enter the new market with the premium positioning and USP; targeted digital promotion; keep selective (direct/online) distribution to protect the brand.
#Operations
Scale up gradually with quality control; automation to meet demand and cut unit cost without sacrificing quality; keep some premium lines carefully managed.
#Finance
Fund via retained earnings + a moderate loan (low gearing, keeps control), staged to manage cash.
#Judgement
Supported, integrated recommendation that balances growth with brand protection and financial prudence; phase the expansion to control quality and risk. Use figures (margin, break-even, low debt).
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, synoptic, uses data, justified recommendation.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

6.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
6.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how budgets can be used to measure performance.
ans: Actual results compared with budget targets; variances show whether departments/managers met targets and where to act. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two drawbacks of using budgets.
ans: Any: time-consuming, may be inaccurate, can demotivate if unrealistic, rigid/discourage flexibility, encourage ‘spending up to budget’. 1–2 + 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘venture capital’.
ans: Finance provided by investors to high-risk, high-potential businesses (1) usually in return for an equity stake (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why a fast-growing tech start-up might prefer venture capital to a bank loan.
ans: No fixed repayments/interest during early loss-making years -> protects cash flow.
Investors bring expertise, contacts and further funding rounds.
Banks may refuse an unproven, asset-light business; but VC means loss of some control/equity.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis using context.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States reasons, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘work–life balance’.
ans: The balance an employee achieves between time/effort spent on work and on personal/family life (1), affecting wellbeing and performance (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways a business could improve the work–life balance of its employees.
ans: Flexible/remote working or flexitime.
Part-time/job-share options; generous leave; limiting overtime.
On-site childcare/wellbeing support.
#Marks
Up to 3 per method (identification + development).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘added value’.
ans: Difference between the price a customer pays and the cost of bought-in inputs (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways a business could increase the value it adds.
ans: Branding/USP to justify a higher price; improved design/features.
Reducing input costs (bulk buying/efficiency) without cutting price.
#Marks
Up to 3 per way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘mass customisation’.
ans: Using flexible (often automated) production (1) to produce large volumes of products tailored to individual customer preferences (1) at near mass-production cost (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit of mass customisation to a business.
ans: Combines economies of scale with personalisation -> customer satisfaction and premium potential without full job-production cost. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between fixed costs and variable costs.
ans: Fixed costs: do not change with output (e.g. rent) (2).
Variable costs: change directly with output (e.g. materials) (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between direct and indirect costs.
ans: Direct: can be attributed to a specific product/cost centre (e.g. direct materials); indirect (overheads): cannot (e.g. admin). 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems that high labour turnover can cause a business.
ans: Higher recruitment and training costs; loss of experienced staff/knowledge.
Disruption to output/quality and lower morale among remaining staff.
Poor customer service/continuity.
#Marks
Up to 3 per problem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one situation in which some labour turnover is beneficial.
ans: Brings in fresh ideas/skills, removes underperformers, allows flexibility/cost adjustment. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between Herzberg’s ‘motivators’ and ‘hygiene factors’.
ans: Motivators (e.g. achievement, recognition, responsibility) cause satisfaction/positive motivation (2).
Hygiene factors (e.g. pay, conditions, supervision) cause dissatisfaction if poor but do not motivate if present (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one implication of Herzberg’s theory for job design.
ans: Enrich jobs (more responsibility/achievement) to motivate, not just improve pay/conditions. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘market segmentation’.
ans: Dividing a market into distinct groups with similar characteristics/needs (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits of market segmentation.
ans: More precise targeting -> less waste/higher response.
Tailored products/prices -> higher satisfaction/premium.
#Marks
Up to 3 per benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘price discrimination’.
ans: Charging different prices to different customers/segments for the same product (1) based on their willingness/ability to pay (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one example of psychological pricing and why it works.
ans: Pricing at $9.99 rather than $10 makes it seem cheaper (left-digit effect), encouraging purchase. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the reasons why small businesses continue to survive alongside large firms in many industries.
ans: Serve niche markets too small for large firms; personal/flexible service.
Local knowledge, close customer relationships, rapid response.
Some industries have few economies of scale (crafts, personal services).
Act as suppliers/subcontractors to large firms.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of several survival factors, applied.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some analysis.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Lists reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether limited liability is the most important factor when choosing a form of business ownership.
ans: For: protects personal assets, encourages investment/risk-taking, aids raising capital.
Against: other factors may matter more – control, cost/complexity of setup, tax, privacy of accounts, ability to raise finance, continuity, nature/size of business.

Judgement: importance depends on the risk of the venture and owner’s circumstances; for high-risk/capital-hungry ventures liability is key, for a small low-risk trader control/simplicity may dominate.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement with context.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited two-sided.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the difference between marketing a good and marketing a service.
ans: Services are intangible, perishable, variable and inseparable from the provider.
Marketing a service stresses staff, reputation, reassurance and experience; goods stress features/packaging.
Quality is harder to standardise for services.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Investing in product development is the most effective way to grow sales.’ Evaluate.
ans: For: new/improved products meet changing needs, differentiate, extend life cycle, justify premium prices.
Against: expensive and risky (many launches fail); promotion, pricing, place or new markets may grow sales more cheaply.
Judgement: depends on market maturity and competition; development matters but is one option among the mix. Not automatically the most effective.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a business could use the product life cycle to plan its marketing.
ans: Different mix at each stage: heavy promotion/skimming or penetration at introduction; build distribution in growth.
Extension strategies in maturity; harvest/withdraw in decline.
Manage a portfolio so new products replace declining ones.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether penetration pricing is the best strategy for launching a new product in a competitive market.
ans: For: gains share/volume quickly, deters entrants, economies of scale, suits price-sensitive mass market.
Against: low margins/slow payback, may signal low quality, hard to raise price later, price war risk; skimming/competitive/value pricing may suit innovative or premium products.
Judgement: best where the market is price-sensitive and scale matters; not best for differentiated/innovative goods. Depends on product and rivals.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse why a dynamic business environment creates both opportunities and threats for entrepreneurs.
ans: Change (technology, consumer tastes, competition, regulation, economy) continually reshapes markets.
Opportunities: new products/markets, e-commerce reach, first-mover advantage.
Threats: disruption of existing products, new competitors, rising costs, obsolescence.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of change producing both effects.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some analysis.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Businesses fail mainly because of factors outside the entrepreneur’s control.’ Evaluate this statement.
ans: For external factors: recession, rising interest rates, new legislation, pandemics, competitor actions, supplier failure.
For internal factors: poor cash-flow control, weak management, inadequate research, over-trading, wrong pricing – all controllable.
Judgement: external shocks trigger failure but well-managed firms with cash reserves and planning survive them; internal weakness usually decisive. Depends on severity of shock and firm resilience.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Supported judgement, balanced, contextual.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘niche market’.
ans: A small, specific segment of a larger market with particular needs (2).

parts.text: Using Table 1, calculate BrightBrew’s market share.
ans: 2 method + 1 answer (≈1.2%).

parts.text: Identify the segmentation base BrightBrew mainly uses, and justify your answer.
ans: Demographic/psychographic (1) – targets high-income (top 20%) and environmentally conscious/lifestyle consumers (2).

parts.text: Explain how the bean shortage (Fig 1) is likely to affect BrightBrew’s costs and pricing.
ans: Reduced supply raises the market price of beans -> higher input costs.
BrightBrew may raise prices (premium buyers less price-sensitive) or absorb costs, cutting margins.
1–2 use of diagram + 2 development.

parts.text: Analyse the benefits to BrightBrew of its customer relationship marketing.
ans: High repeat-purchase (68%) via subscription -> stable revenue and high customer lifetime value.
Personalisation raises satisfaction/loyalty and word-of-mouth, defending its niche against big rivals.
Customer data guides product/marketing decisions.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis using case data.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.text: Recommend whether BrightBrew should move into the mass market or stay in its premium niche. Justify your recommendation.
ans: #For mass market
Access to a large, growing ($260m, +12%) market and economies of scale; recession makes cheaper pods attractive.
#For staying niche
Head-to-head competition with two dominant mass firms is risky/costly; would dilute its ethical premium brand and lose its 68% loyalty; premium buyers are less hit by recession.
#Judgement

Supported recommendation, e.g. remain in and deepen the profitable niche via CRM (its core strength) rather than compete on price with giants; perhaps a limited premium supermarket range rather than full mass market. Weigh brand identity vs scale.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses data, justified recommendation.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

7.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
7.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between an autocratic and a democratic management style.
ans: Autocratic: manager makes decisions alone and directs staff (2).
Democratic: manager consults and involves staff in decisions (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain McGregor’s Theory X view of workers.
ans: Theory X assumes workers dislike work, avoid responsibility and must be controlled/directed and motivated by money/threat. 3 marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘capacity utilisation’.
ans: Percentage of maximum output currently being used (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A firm produces 8,400 units against a maximum of 12,000. Calculate capacity utilisation and explain one problem of low utilisation.
ans: Low utilisation spreads fixed costs over few units -> high unit cost/low profit.
2 calc + up to 3 explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two uses of break-even analysis.
ans: Any two: set output/sales targets, assess effect of price/cost changes, support finance applications, judge margin of safety, aid decision-making.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse two limitations of break-even analysis.
ans: Assumes all output is sold and costs/price are constant (linear) – unrealistic.
Ignores discounts/economies of scale; only as good as the data; static (one snapshot).
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two limitations analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies limitations, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline McClelland’s three needs.
ans: Need for achievement, need for affiliation (belonging) and need for power (3 marks; 1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how understanding McClelland’s needs could help a manager assign roles.
ans: Match roles to dominant need – achievers get challenging targets, affiliation types get teamwork, power types get leadership. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘intrapreneurship’.
ans: Employees within an existing business (1) behaving like entrepreneurs – taking initiative, innovating and developing new ideas/products (1) using company resources, without bearing personal financial risk (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how intrapreneurship can contribute to the ongoing success of an established business.
ans: Generates a flow of new products/processes that keep the firm competitive as markets change.
Improves motivation and retention of talented staff (empowerment, ownership of ideas).
Helps a large business remain dynamic and avoid complacency/decline.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed chains of analysis linking intrapreneurship to sustained competitiveness.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States benefits with limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the interaction of demand and supply determines the market price.
ans: Price settles at equilibrium where quantity demanded = quantity supplied.
Excess demand pushes price up; excess supply pushes it down until they balance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw and label a demand and supply diagram showing equilibrium price and quantity.
ans: Axes: price (y), quantity (x); downward demand, upward supply; intersection marked P and Q. 3 marks for correct, labelled diagram.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the five levels of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, from lowest to highest.
ans: Physiological -> safety/security -> social/love & belonging -> esteem -> self-actualisation (3 marks for correct order).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how a manager could use Maslow’s hierarchy to motivate staff.
ans: Meet lower needs first: fair pay (physiological), secure contracts/safe conditions (safety).
Then social (teamwork), esteem (recognition/status) and self-actualisation (challenging work/development).
Motivators must match the level an individual is currently seeking.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Applies each level to workplace practice.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Lists levels, limited application.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Budgeted sales revenue was $200,000; actual sales were $224,000. Calculate the variance and state its type.
ans: =Variance = 224,000 − 200,000 = $24,000 higher revenue -> $24,000 FAVOURABLE
2 calc + 1 type.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit of investigating variances.
ans: Identifies problems/successes early -> corrective action and better future budgets/control. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the ‘transformational process’.
ans: The process of converting inputs (resources) into outputs (goods/services) (1) that have greater value to customers (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using an example, how a bakery adds value through the transformational process.
ans: Inputs: flour, labour, ovens (capital), enterprise.
Transformation: mixing and baking turns cheap ingredients into bread/cakes.
Output sells for far more than input cost -> value added.
Up to 5 for applied explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘crowdfunding’.
ans: Raising small amounts of finance from a large number of people (1), usually via an online platform (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit and one drawback of crowdfunding for a start-up.
ans: Benefit: access to finance without banks, market validation/publicity. Drawback: no guarantee of reaching target, idea exposed to competitors, fees. 2 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a business could become more market-orientated.
ans: Conduct market research to identify customer needs and monitor trends.
Involve marketing in product development; use customer feedback/CRM data.
Adjust the marketing mix to match customer wants.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the view that customer relationship marketing is worth the investment for all businesses.
ans: For: loyalty, repeat purchase, higher lifetime value, cheaper than winning new customers, referrals, useful data.
Against: costly systems/time; low value for one-off/low-frequency purchases; data/privacy risks; not all customers want a ‘relationship’.
Judgement: worthwhile where repeat purchase and customer lifetime value are high (e.g. banking, subscriptions); less so for infrequent low-value goods.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how good employee welfare can improve business performance.
ans: Better wellbeing -> lower absence/turnover and higher productivity.
Improved morale, loyalty and reputation aid recruitment.
Fewer disputes and accidents; better customer service.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the view that trade unions are more of a threat than a benefit to a business.
ans: Threat: potential strikes/disruption, higher wage costs, restrictive practices, slower change.
Benefit: efficient communication/bargaining channel, fewer individual disputes, improved morale/representation, partnership can raise productivity.
Judgement: depends on the relationship (adversarial vs partnership) and management approach; unions can be a benefit if relations are cooperative.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a business could respond to a large adverse cost variance.
ans: Investigate the cause (prices, waste, volume, efficiency).
Take corrective action: renegotiate supplies, cut waste, improve productivity, revise processes.
Adjust future budgets if the assumption was wrong.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Accurate budgeting is impossible, so budgets are a waste of time.’ Evaluate this statement.
ans: For: forecasts are estimates; unexpected events cause variances; time/cost of preparation.
Against: budgets still guide planning, control, motivation and finance; variances are informative even when budgets are imperfect; flexible budgets cope with change.
Judgement: perfect accuracy is not the aim – budgets add value as planning and control tools if realistic and reviewed; not a waste of time.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how strong branding can benefit a business.
ans: Recognition, trust and loyalty -> repeat purchase and premium pricing.
Easier launch of new products (brand extension); differentiation; bargaining power with retailers.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘The product is the most important element of the marketing mix.’ Evaluate this view.
ans: For product: without a good product meeting needs, price/promotion/place cannot succeed; USP drives everything.
Against: a great product fails with wrong price, poor promotion or unavailability; the Ps are interdependent; in some markets price/place dominate.
Judgement: product is fundamental but not sufficient; the whole, consistent mix matters. Importance varies by market.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘product portfolio’.
ans: The range/collection of products a business sells (1) across different markets/segments (1).

parts.text: Using Table 1, classify each of the four products using the Boston Matrix.
ans: ClassicPhone = Cash cow (low growth, high share).
FoldX = Question mark (high growth, low share).
Smart-watch = Star (high growth, high share).
MP3 player = Dog (low growth, low share).
1 mark each.

parts.text: Explain why ClassicPhone is described as generating ‘strong cash’ despite low market growth.
ans: High share in a mature market gives high sales with low investment need (no growth to fund).
Established product, economies of scale, low promotion cost -> net cash inflow (cash cow).
1–2 + development.

parts.text: Analyse whether price skimming or penetration pricing is more suitable for the FoldX launch.
ans: Skimming: patented technology, few competitors, early adopters pay premium, recovers R&D.
Penetration: builds share fast in a high-growth market but sacrifices margin and may not suit a premium/innovative product.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Weighs both using the case.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States methods, limited application.

parts.text: Analyse how Aurora could use the cash from ClassicPhone to strengthen its portfolio.
