ans: Reinvest in the star (smart-watch) and question mark (FoldX) to build/keep share in growing markets.
Fund R&D/promotion so FoldX becomes a future star; consider dropping the MP3 dog.
Balances the portfolio for long-term revenue as ClassicPhone eventually declines.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis using Boston logic and the case.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.text: Recommend a marketing strategy for FoldX, including pricing and promotion. Justify your recommendation using the case.
ans: #Pricing
Skimming suits its patented tech and premium positioning; lower later as rivals enter.
#Promotion
Digital and targeted launch to early adopters/tech enthusiasts; stress USP (foldable innovation).
#Portfolio link
Fund the launch from ClassicPhone cash; aim to convert the question mark into a star in the high-growth market.
#Judgement

Supported recommendation weighing margin vs share; e.g. skim initially to fund investment and signal premium quality, then reduce price to build share as the market grows. Acknowledge risk of rivals/patents expiring.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses case, justified recommendation across the mix.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

8.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
8.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why businesses fail.
ans: Any two: poor cash-flow/liquidity management; lack of finance; poor management; insufficient market research/no demand; strong competition; over-expansion; external shocks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why a shortage of cash is often a more immediate cause of failure than low profit.
ans: A profitable business can still run out of cash (e.g. cash tied up in receivables or inventory) and be unable to pay suppliers/wages/loans.
Insolvency triggers legal action, loss of supplier credit and ultimately liquidation – quickly.
Low profit is a longer-term/structural problem that can be corrected over time if cash continues to flow.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Analyses the cash-vs-profit distinction and links liquidity to survival.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Describes cash and profit with limited analysis of urgency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between an incremental budget and a zero-based budget.
ans: Incremental: based on last period’s budget adjusted (e.g. +5%) (2).
Zero-based: every item must be justified from zero each period (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of zero-based budgeting.
ans: Avoids carrying forward waste/unnecessary spending; forces justification and efficient allocation. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘enterprise’ as a factor of production.
ans: The willingness and ability of an entrepreneur (1) to organise the other factors of production and take the risk of producing goods/services for profit (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two qualities an entrepreneur needs to succeed.
ans: Risk-taking/resilience – willing to commit resources despite uncertain returns and recover from setbacks.
Innovation/creativity – spots gaps in the market and develops new solutions.
Determination, self-confidence, effective multi-tasking or leadership are equally valid.
#Marks
Up to 3 marks per quality: 1 for identification, 2 for developed explanation of why it aids success.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘working capital’.
ans: The finance available for day-to-day operations (1); current assets minus current liabilities (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why managing working capital is important to a business.
ans: Ensures enough liquidity to pay suppliers, wages and short-term debts.
Too little -> insolvency risk; too much -> idle cash/inventory (opportunity cost).
Affects supplier/creditor relationships and survival.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of importance.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States importance, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a favourable variance is not always a good sign.
ans: Lower spending might mean cut corners/quality (e.g. cheaper materials) or under-investment that harms the business later; may reflect an unrealistic budget. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one link between budgets and a business’s objectives.
ans: Budgets translate objectives into departmental financial targets/resources to achieve them. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how budgets can motivate or demotivate employees.
ans: Realistic, participative targets can motivate (ownership, clear goals).
Unrealistic/imposed targets or blame for adverse variances can demotivate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why involving managers in setting budgets can be beneficial.
ans: Increases accuracy (local knowledge), ownership and commitment to targets. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘marketing objective’.
ans: A specific marketing goal a business wants to achieve (1), e.g. to raise market share or brand awareness, that supports corporate objectives (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the link between marketing objectives and corporate objectives.
ans: Corporate objectives (e.g. growth) set the overall direction.
Marketing objectives (e.g. +10% market share) are derived to help achieve them.
They must be consistent so marketing activity supports overall strategy.
Up to 5 for developed explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between product orientation and market (customer) orientation.
ans: Product-orientated: focuses on the product/what the firm can make (2).
Market-orientated: focuses on identifying and meeting customer needs (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one risk of being product-orientated.
ans: May produce goods customers do not want -> unsold stock/lost sales; ignores changing tastes. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘workforce plan’.
ans: A plan that forecasts the number and type of employees a business will need (1) and how it will obtain and retain them (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse two factors a business must consider when producing a workforce plan.
ans: Forecast demand for products/expected growth or decline.
Labour turnover/retirements and skills required; labour market availability.
Technology/automation changing skill needs; budget.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two factors analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies factors, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two methods of measuring the size of a business.
ans: Any two: number of employees; revenue/sales turnover; capital employed; market share; market capitalisation; value of output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why different methods of measuring business size can give conflicting results.
ans: A capital-intensive firm (e.g. oil refinery) has high capital employed but few employees.
A labour-intensive firm (e.g. call centre) employs many but has modest turnover.
So ‘largest’ depends on the measure chosen; no single measure is best.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Analyses contradictions with examples.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Lists methods, limited analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse why operating persistently at 100% capacity could be a problem for a business.
ans: No slack for extra orders, maintenance or breakdowns -> missed sales/deliveries.
Overworked staff/machines -> quality falls, stress, higher turnover, breakdowns.
Signals need to expand capacity (investment).
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate how a rapidly growing business should best increase its capacity.
ans: Options: overtime/extra shifts (fast, flexible, but higher wage cost/fatigue), invest in machinery/premises (long-term, costly, needs finance), outsource (flexible, less control).
Judgement: short-term/uncertain growth favours overtime/outsourcing; sustained growth justifies investment; depends on finance, demand certainty and lead time.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a business could use both quantitative and qualitative research to plan a product launch.
ans: Quantitative (surveys) sizes demand, price points, market share potential.
Qualitative (focus groups) explains preferences, image, reasons and reactions to prototypes.
Combined, they reduce risk and shape the mix.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the reliability of the results a business can obtain from sampling.
ans: For: well-designed random/stratified samples of adequate size give representative, cost-effective results.
Against: sampling/selection bias, small samples, poor question design and non-response reduce reliability; can mislead.
Judgement: reliability depends on sample size, method and design; sampling is necessary and can be reliable if done well, but results carry a margin of error.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a horizontal merger could benefit two competing supermarket chains.
ans: Increased market share/market power and reduced competition.
Economies of scale (purchasing, distribution, marketing) lowering unit costs.
Rationalisation of duplicated functions/sites; wider geographic coverage.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis of merger benefits.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some analysis.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the impact of a hostile takeover on the stakeholders of the target business.
ans: Employees: job losses/uncertainty vs possible investment and new opportunities.
Shareholders: often a premium price vs loss of independence.
Managers: may be replaced; customers/suppliers: changed terms, prices, standards.
Judgement: impact varies by stakeholder and depends on acquirer intentions and integration; often negative short-term for staff, mixed long-term.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced across stakeholders with judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the importance of a clear employment contract to both employer and employee.
ans: Employer: sets duties, hours, notice, and grounds for discipline – legal protection.
Employee: clarifies pay, rights, holiday and security – reduces disputes.
Reduces misunderstanding and provides a basis for fair dismissal/redundancy.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis for both parties.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of online recruitment compared with traditional methods for a small business.
ans: For online: cheap, wide/fast reach, easy to filter, targets specific skills.
Against: huge volume of unsuitable applicants, may miss local/older candidates, screening time, less personal.
Judgement: depends on role, budget and target labour market; often best combined with local/agency methods for a small firm.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘added value’ (as used by Amara).
ans: Difference between selling price and cost of bought-in inputs/materials (2).

parts.text: Using Table 1, calculate the value added per bottle by LiveCulture.
ans: =Bought-in materials = ingredients $0.70 + packaging $0.35 = $1.05
=Added value = price $3.00 − $1.05 = $1.95 per bottle
Accept $1.95 (2 method + 1 answer). If labour/other variable also deducted and clearly labelled as contribution, note distinction: contribution = $3.00 − $1.70 = $1.30.

parts.text: Explain, using the concept of opportunity cost, the true cost to Amara of leaving her job to start LiveCulture.
ans: Opportunity cost = next best alternative foregone.
By leaving, Amara sacrifices her $42,000 salary (and job security) – an implicit cost not shown in the accounts.
Her $25,000 savings also lose the interest/return they could have earned elsewhere.
1–2 for concept, up to 2 for applied figures.

parts.text: Analyse two qualities Amara has shown that are associated with successful entrepreneurs.
ans: Risk-taking: left a secure salaried job and committed $25,000 savings plus a $30,000 loan.
Planning/organisation: wrote a detailed business plan; combines factors of production.
Innovation/marketing insight: builds added value through branding and a health image.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two qualities analysed with clear use of the case.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies qualities, limited application.

parts.text: Analyse why LiveCulture was profitable yet almost ran out of cash in its first year.
ans: Profit is revenue minus expenses (accruals); cash is actual money in/out and timing differs.
Cafes pay 60 days after delivery (trade receivables) so cash is tied up while Amara must pay ingredients, wages and the loan now.
Loan repayments and stock-building consume cash but are not full expenses of the period.
Year-end cash of only $1,900 shows a liquidity problem despite $26,000 profit – risk of insolvency.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of the cash-vs-profit gap using case data (receivables, timing).
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some analysis of the distinction.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|States cash ≠ profit.

parts.text: Amara must decide whether to accept the supermarket order. Recommend whether she should accept it. Justify your answer using the case and your knowledge.
ans: #Case for accepting
Large sales/scale increase, economies of scale, higher brand exposure, long-term growth.
#Case against / risks

Requires a further loan (rising debt/interest) when cash is already tight; supermarkets demand low prices and long credit terms, worsening the cash-flow gap; capacity and quality risk; dependence on one powerful customer.
#Judgement

A supported decision, e.g. accept only if payment terms/an overdraft facility are negotiated to protect liquidity, or grow more slowly; recognise the existing cash-flow weakness is the key constraint.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses case data, clear justified recommendation.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement, some application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two-sided, limited application/judgement.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

9.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
9.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘franchise’.
ans: An arrangement where the franchisee buys the right (1) to use an established business’s name, products and format (1) in return for a fee/royalty (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one drawback of buying a franchise for the franchisee.
ans: Loss of independence/must follow rules; ongoing royalties reduce profit; reputation depends on other franchisees. 1 + 2 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of a private limited company (Ltd).
ans: Any two: shares not sold to the public/traded on a stock exchange; shares transferred privately with agreement; separate legal identity; limited liability; must file accounts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages of forming a private limited company rather than remaining a partnership.
ans: Limited liability protects owners’ personal assets.
Easier to raise capital by issuing shares to family/investors.
Continuity – separate legal identity survives death of an owner.
#Marks
Up to 3 per advantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a job description and a person specification.
ans: Job description: details the duties/tasks and responsibilities of the role (2).
Person specification: the skills, qualifications and qualities the ideal candidate needs (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person specification is useful in the selection process.
ans: Provides objective criteria to shortlist/compare candidates and reduce bias/mismatch. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘variance’.
ans: The difference between a budgeted (planned) figure and the actual figure (1) for income or costs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between a favourable and an adverse variance.
ans: Favourable: actual result is better than budget (higher revenue/profit or lower cost) (2).
Adverse: actual result is worse than budget (lower revenue/profit or higher cost) (2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘job enrichment’.
ans: Redesigning a job to include more challenging, meaningful tasks and responsibility (1) to increase motivation (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two non-financial methods (other than job enrichment) a business could use to motivate staff.
ans: Empowerment/participation; teamworking; job rotation/enlargement.
Opportunities for training, promotion and status; recognition.
#Marks
Up to 3 per method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what ‘SMART’ objectives stands for.
ans: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-limited (all five for 2; 3–4 for 1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why setting SMART objectives can improve business performance.
ans: Clear targets focus effort and aid coordination.
Measurable/time-limited allows performance to be monitored and corrective action taken.
Achievable/realistic targets motivate rather than demoralise staff.
1 per point developed, max 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘contribution’ (per unit).
ans: Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit (1); it contributes towards fixed costs and then profit (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A product sells for $20 with variable cost $12. Calculate contribution per unit and total contribution from 5,000 units.
ans: =Contribution per unit = 20 − 12 = $8
=Total contribution = 8 × 5,000 = $40,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between efficiency and effectiveness.
ans: Efficiency: producing output with the least waste of resources/cost (2).
Effectiveness: achieving the intended objective/meeting customer needs (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a business can be efficient but not effective.
ans: It may produce cheaply/quickly (efficient) but make the wrong product that customers don’t want (not effective). 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between cash and profit.
ans: Profit = revenue minus expenses over a period (accruals).
Cash = actual money flowing in/out; timing differs (e.g. credit sales, loan repayments), so a profitable firm can run short of cash.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason a profitable business might still fail.
ans: Liquidity crisis – cash tied up in receivables/inventory, cannot pay bills -> insolvency/liquidation. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a merger and a takeover.
ans: Merger: two firms agree to combine into one new entity (2).
Takeover: one firm acquires a controlling interest in another, which may be friendly or hostile (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify and explain one example of vertical (backward) integration.
ans: A manufacturer buying its raw-material supplier (e.g. a coffee chain buying a coffee plantation) to secure supply/reduce costs. 1 example + 2 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how effective supply chain management can improve a business’s competitiveness.
ans: Lower input costs and lead times -> lower prices/faster delivery.
Reliable quality and availability -> customer satisfaction/retention.
Resilience and flexibility to respond to demand changes.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the view that holding buffer inventory is a waste of money.
ans: For: buffer stock ties up cash, incurs storage/obsolescence cost, and can hide inefficiency.
Against: protects against stock-outs, delivery delays and demand spikes; avoids costly lost sales/production halts; vital where supply is unreliable.
Judgement: not a waste if it prevents greater losses; the right buffer balances holding cost against stock-out cost. Depends on supply reliability and demand volatility.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse why the selection process is as important as the recruitment process.
ans: Recruitment attracts a pool; selection chooses the right person – a poor choice is costly.
Wrong selection -> low productivity, higher turnover, retraining, morale/legal issues.
Good selection (valid methods) matches person to person specification.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Making workers redundant is always bad for a business.’ Evaluate this view.
ans: For: lowers morale/loyalty, loss of skills, redundancy cost, reputation, survivor stress, risk of losing needed staff in an upturn.
Against: cuts costs, improves competitiveness/survival, allows restructuring, may be unavoidable in decline.
Judgement: depends on necessity, how it is handled (fair procedure, voluntary first, support) and whether skills will be needed again. Sometimes essential for survival.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the traditional functions of management identified by Fayol.
ans: Planning (setting objectives/direction), organising (resources/structure).
Directing/commanding (leading & motivating staff), controlling (monitoring vs targets and correcting).
Coordinating activities across the business.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of the functions and their contribution.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Lists functions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether financial rewards are the best way to motivate a workforce.
ans: For (Taylor): pay drives effort, easy to link to output (piece rate/bonus/PRP), meets lower needs.
Against (Mayo/Maslow/Herzberg): money is a hygiene factor; social, esteem and self-actualisation needs and job design matter; over-reliance harms quality/teamwork.
Judgement: depends on the type of work, the individual and pay level; a mix of financial and non-financial usually best. Money necessary but not sufficient.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement using theory.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse why a business’s objectives may change over its life or with a change in the economic environment.
ans: Start-up survival -> growth -> profit maximisation as it matures.
Recession may shift focus to survival/cash; boom to growth/market share.
New owners, competition or CSR pressures reshape objectives.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis with examples.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the importance to a business of accountability to its stakeholders.
ans: For: builds trust, reduces conflict, meets legal/ethical duties, protects reputation and access to finance/labour.
Against: accountability to many groups is costly, can slow decisions and create conflicting demands; some stakeholders have little power.
Judgement: accountability matters most where stakeholder power/interest is high; selective, prioritised accountability is realistic.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘working capital’.
ans: Current assets minus current liabilities – finance for day-to-day operations (2).

parts.text: Using Table 1, calculate Nova’s working capital.
ans: =Working capital = current assets $1.9m − current liabilities $1.4m = $0.5m
2 method + 1 answer ($0.5m).

parts.text: Explain why Nova can be profitable yet short of cash.
ans: Customers pay after 60 days (receivables $1.1m) but Nova pays suppliers in 30 days and is building inventory -> cash outflows precede inflows.
Profit ($620k) is earned on paper before the cash arrives.
1–2 + development using the case.

parts.text: Explain one way Nova could improve its cash position from working capital.
ans: Reduce receivables (shorter credit terms/factoring/prompt-payment discounts), or negotiate longer supplier credit, or cut inventory.
1–2 + development.

parts.text: Analyse two suitable sources of finance for the $1.3m expansion (showrooms + machinery).
ans: Bank loan: long-term, matches long-life assets, keeps ownership; but interest and repayments add fixed cost when cash is tight.
Sale and leaseback of the warehouse: releases a large lump sum without new debt or dilution; but loses the asset and adds rent.
New shares to an investor: no repayments but dilutes control (owners want to keep control).
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Two sources analysed against Nova’s needs/constraints.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.text: Recommend how Nova should finance the $1.3m expansion. Justify your recommendation using the case and data.
ans: #Consider constraints
Owners want to keep control (avoid new shares) and are cautious about debt; retained earnings only $350k; cash is tight.
#Options
Use $350k retained earnings + a bank loan for the rest (keeps control, matches long-term assets) or sale and leaseback (avoids debt but loses asset/adds rent).
#Judgement

Supported recommendation, e.g. combine retained earnings with a moderate bank loan (low existing gearing at $0.3m makes debt affordable) while fixing the receivables gap to protect cash; avoid diluting control. Justify with figures.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses data, justified recommendation respecting owners’ aims.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

10.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
10.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two barriers to entrepreneurship.
ans: Any two: lack of finance/capital; lack of business skills or experience; high competition; fear of failure; complex regulation/red tape; lack of a viable idea; limited access to markets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a lack of finance acts as a barrier to entrepreneurship.
ans: Start-ups need capital for premises, equipment and initial stock, plus cash for early losses.
Without savings, collateral or a track record, lenders/investors are reluctant, so the venture may never launch or is under-resourced and fails.
1–2 for identification, up to 2 further for developed chain of reasoning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline Vroom’s expectancy theory (process theory).
ans: Motivation depends on expectancy (effort leads to performance), instrumentality (performance leads to reward) and valence (value of the reward) (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way a manager could raise motivation using expectancy theory.
ans: Ensure effort is achievable, link performance clearly to rewards, and offer rewards employees actually value. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘flexible budget’.
ans: A budget that is adjusted to reflect the actual level of activity/output (1), so costs are compared at the achieved output (1) rather than the original planned output (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a flexible budget can give a fairer measure of performance.
ans: It compares actual costs with what they should be at the actual output, isolating true over/under-spending from volume differences. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘tertiary sector’.
ans: The sector providing services (1) to businesses and consumers, e.g. retail, banking, transport, insurance (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the relative importance of the secondary sector has declined in many high-income economies.
ans: De-industrialisation: manufacturing shifts to lower-cost countries (globalisation).
Rising incomes raise demand for services (tourism, finance, leisure).
Automation reduces manufacturing employment; growth of the quaternary/knowledge economy.
#Marks
Up to 3 per reason (identification + development).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one problem of operating at or above maximum capacity for a long period.
ans: No slack for extra orders/maintenance; overworked staff/machines -> breakdowns, quality falls, stress, missed deliveries. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways a business could increase its capacity.
ans: Any: invest in more machinery/premises, hire more staff, add shifts/overtime, outsource, improve productivity. 1–2 + 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘multi-skilling’.
ans: Training employees to perform several different tasks/roles (1), increasing flexibility of the workforce (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit and one drawback of multi-skilling for a manufacturer.
ans: Benefit: flexible cover, fewer bottlenecks. Drawback: training cost, possible demand for higher pay. 2 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between risk and uncertainty.
ans: Risk: an outcome that can be identified and the probability estimated/insured against (2).
Uncertainty: unpredictable events that cannot be foreseen or measured, e.g. a sudden change in government policy or a pandemic (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way an entrepreneur could reduce business risk.
ans: Market research to test demand before committing (reduces likelihood of unsold output).
Or: writing a business plan, insurance, starting small/pilot. 1 mark method + up to 2 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between mass marketing and niche marketing.
ans: Mass: aiming a product at the whole/large market with a standardised offer (2).
Niche: targeting a small, specific segment with a specialised offer (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of niche marketing for a small business.
ans: Less direct competition from large firms, can charge premium prices, closer customer relationships, lower marketing spend. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two factors that influence the demand for a product.
ans: Any two: price, incomes, price of substitutes/complements, tastes/fashion, advertising, season, population.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a rise in consumer incomes could affect demand for a luxury car.
ans: Luxury cars are a normal/luxury good, so higher incomes raise demand (shift right); consumers can afford more premium goods. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘re-order level’.
ans: The inventory level at which a new order is automatically placed (1) to replenish stock before it runs out (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: On an inventory control chart, explain what the gap between maximum inventory and buffer inventory represents.
ans: The usable/working stock that is drawn down between deliveries; the re-order quantity brings it back to maximum. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the reasons for the growing importance of the quaternary sector in developed economies.
ans: Knowledge/information economy: R&D, ICT, consultancy, education.
Technological change and digitalisation create high-value services.
Rising incomes and demand for innovation; competitive advantage from knowledge.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some analysis.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A successful sole trader is considering converting to a public limited company (plc). Evaluate this decision.
ans: For: access to large-scale equity finance via stock market, limited liability, status, ability to grow.
Against: loss of control (dilution, possible takeover), heavy regulation/disclosure costs, short-termism/shareholder pressure, divorce of ownership and control, flotation cost.
Judgement: appropriate only if large capital is genuinely needed and the owner accepts reduced control; otherwise an Ltd may be a better intermediate step.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement, contextual.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the benefits and drawbacks of flow production for a car manufacturer.
ans: Benefits: low unit cost at volume, consistent quality, high output, automation.
Drawbacks: huge set-up cost, inflexibility, breakdown risk halts line, demotivating work.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis both sides.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the impact on a business of investing to make its operations more sustainable.
ans: For: lower long-run energy/waste costs, reputation/brand, meets regulation and customer/investor demand, risk reduction.
Against: high upfront cost, longer payback, possible higher short-term unit cost, uncertain returns, competitors may not.
Judgement: increasingly worthwhile as regulation/consumer pressure rise; depends on cost, payback and market; net positive long-term for many firms.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the costs and benefits to a business of holding high levels of inventory.
ans: Benefits: avoids stock-outs/lost sales, buffers against delivery/demand fluctuations, bulk discounts, smooth production.
Costs: storage, insurance, obsolescence, and cash tied up (opportunity cost).
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis both sides.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether a manufacturer should adopt a JIT approach to inventory.
ans: For: cuts holding costs, frees cash/space, reduces waste/obsolescence, encourages efficiency and quality.
Against: highly vulnerable to supply disruption (strikes, transport, global shocks), needs reliable suppliers and forecasting, loses bulk discounts, stock-out risk.
Judgement: suits stable demand and reliable supply chains; risky where supply is uncertain – many now hold some buffer (hybrid). Depends on context.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the difference between cash and profit and why it matters to managers.
ans: Profit is an accounting measure (accruals); cash is actual liquidity/timing.
Credit sales, stock-building and loan repayments create gaps between the two.
Managers must manage both – profit for viability, cash for survival.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the usefulness of leasing rather than buying non-current assets outright.
ans: For leasing: no large upfront cash outlay, protects working capital, up-to-date equipment, maintenance often included.
Against: total cost usually higher over time, asset never owned, ongoing commitment.
Judgement: leasing suits cash-tight or fast-changing-tech situations; buying suits long-life assets when finance is available. Depends on cash position and asset type.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘capital-intensive production’.
ans: Production that relies mainly on machinery/technology rather than labour (2).

parts.text: Using Table 1, calculate labour productivity (tiles per worker per week) for the Artisan range.
ans: =2,000 / 25 = 80 tiles per worker per week
2 method + 1 answer (80).

parts.text: Using Table 1, calculate the added value per tile for the Everyday range.
ans: =Added value per Everyday tile = price $3.50 − unit cost $1.10 = $2.40 (accept price minus bought-in cost basis).
Note: Artisan added value per tile = $11.00 − $4.20 = $6.80.
2 method + 1 answer.

parts.text: Explain one reason Terra wants to keep the Artisan range labour-intensive.
ans: Handmade craftsmanship is the brand’s USP -> premium price ($11) and high added value ($6.80).
Automating it could damage the handmade image and quality perception.
1–2 + development.

parts.text: Analyse the benefits to Terra of investing in the automated flow line for the Everyday range.
ans: Massive output rise (2,000 -> 30,000/week) and much lower unit cost ($1.10) -> competes with cheap imports.
Consistent quality, meets growing demand and long lead times, higher total volume.
Frees premium capacity/reputation while capturing the mass market.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis using data.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.text: Recommend whether Terra should proceed with the $1.8m investment and sustainability measures. Justify your answer using the case and data.
ans: #For
Meets demand, low unit cost to fight imports, growth, long-run sustainability savings/reputation.
#Against / risks
$1.8m cost/financing and payback risk; only 8 jobs vs 25 -> possible redundancies/morale; risk to handmade brand if Everyday confuses positioning.
#Judgement

Supported recommendation, e.g. proceed but keep the two ranges/brands clearly separate to protect Artisan’s premium image, redeploy/retrain staff, and stage sustainability spend to manage cash. Weigh growth/competitiveness vs cost and brand risk.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses data, justified recommendation.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

11.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
11.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between financial and non-financial motivators.
ans: Financial: money-based rewards (pay, bonus, commission) (2).
Non-financial: non-monetary methods (job enrichment, recognition, empowerment) (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one non-financial method of motivation.
ans: Job enrichment/empowerment/teamwork/recognition – developed. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘job production’.
ans: Producing one-off/custom items individually to a customer’s specific requirements (1), e.g. a tailored suit or a bridge (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse two advantages of job production.
ans: Meets exact customer needs -> can charge premium prices.
Flexible, high quality, motivating/varied work for staff.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two advantages analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies advantages, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘product differentiation’.
ans: Making a product distinct from rivals (1) through design, features, branding or service (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the importance of product development to a business over time.
ans: Keeps products competitive as tastes/technology change; extends life cycle; supports growth and pricing power. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘trade union’.
ans: An organisation of workers (1) that represents and protects their collective interests in negotiations with employers (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how trade union involvement can benefit both employees and employers.
ans: Employees: collective bargaining power for better pay/conditions and representation in disputes.
Employers: a single channel for negotiation (efficient communication), fewer individual disputes, workforce views heard, aiding cooperation and productivity.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Both sides analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies benefits, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘human resource management (HRM)’.
ans: The management function responsible for recruiting, developing, deploying and retaining employees (1) so the business meets its objectives (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two roles of HRM in helping a business meet its objectives.
ans: Workforce planning – ensures the right number/skills of staff are available when needed.
Recruitment/selection and training – provides capable, motivated staff to raise productivity.
Managing morale/relations – reduces turnover and disputes.
#Marks
Up to 3 per role.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two objectives of promotion.
ans: Any two: inform, persuade, remind, build brand/loyalty, increase sales/market share, launch a product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse the growing importance of digital promotion for businesses.
ans: Wide, targeted reach at lower cost; measurable (analytics); interactive/social.
Personalisation and remarketing; supports e-commerce; but oversupply of ads/ad-blocking and reputation risk.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of digital promotion.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States points, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two internal sources of finance.
ans: Any two: retained earnings/profit, sale of unwanted assets, sale and leaseback, working capital, owner’s investment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse two advantages of using retained earnings to finance expansion.
ans: No interest or repayment; no loss of control (no new shares/lenders).
Quick/flexible; available without approval; no debt on the balance sheet.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two advantages analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies advantages, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between redundancy and dismissal.
ans: Redundancy: job no longer needed (e.g. downsizing) – not the employee’s fault (2).
Dismissal: employment terminated because of the employee’s conduct/capability (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between voluntary and involuntary redundancy.
ans: Voluntary: employees choose to leave (often for a payment); involuntary: employer selects who must go. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how business objectives might change as a business grows.
ans: Start-up: survival/cash flow; established: growth/market share; mature: profit maximisation/shareholder value or CSR.
Objectives change with the economy, competition and ownership.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one way objectives are translated into targets for departments.
ans: Via budgets and departmental/individual targets (e.g. a sales objective becomes a monthly sales budget/quota). 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘customer relationship marketing (CRM)’.
ans: A strategy focused on building long-term relationships with customers (1) to increase loyalty and repeat purchases (1) rather than one-off sales (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one cost and one benefit of CRM.
ans: Benefit: loyalty/repeat sales, higher lifetime value, referrals. Cost: technology/CRM systems, staff time, data management. 2 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how market segmentation could help a clothing retailer increase sales.
ans: Identify segments (age, income, lifestyle) and tailor ranges/prices to each.
Target promotion to the right audience -> higher conversion and loyalty.
Spot underserved segments/new opportunities.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether niche marketing or mass marketing is the better strategy for a new food producer.
ans: Niche: less competition, premium prices, loyal customers, lower initial spend; but small sales, vulnerable if segment shrinks or a big firm enters.
Mass: high volume, economies of scale, brand reach; but heavy competition/spend and needs large capacity/finance.
Judgement: for a new/small producer niche is usually safer initially; depends on finance, capacity and product. Could grow niche -> mass later.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement, contextual.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a business could use the marketing mix to launch a new product successfully.
ans: Product: clear USP meeting researched needs; Price: penetration/skimming as appropriate.
Promotion: targeted (often digital) to build awareness; Place: suitable channels.
The 4Ps must be consistent.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the view that finance is the most important functional area for a new business.
ans: For: without cash/finance the business cannot start, operate or survive; cash-flow failure is a top cause of collapse.
Against: marketing (demand), operations (delivery) and HRM (people) are equally vital; weak in any area causes failure; areas are interdependent.
Judgement: finance is critical for survival, especially early on, but success needs all functions working together. Depends on stage/context.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the importance of joint ventures and strategic alliances as methods of external growth.
ans: Share costs, risks and expertise on a specific project without full merger.
Access to new markets/local knowledge (esp. entering foreign markets).
Retain independence; faster than organic growth.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Growth by takeover rarely achieves its objectives.’ Evaluate this view.
ans: For: culture clashes, overpayment, integration problems, diseconomies of scale, loss of key staff, distraction of management.
Against: can succeed – synergies, market power, economies of scale, faster growth, acquiring capability/brands.
Judgement: success depends on due diligence, price paid, integration planning and strategic fit; many fail but well-planned deals add value. Depends on context.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a business could use break-even analysis to assess the effect of raising its selling price.
ans: Higher price raises contribution per unit -> lowers break-even output and raises margin of safety/profit at a given volume.
But higher price may reduce quantity demanded (not shown on chart) – sales could fall.
Chart shifts: total revenue line steeper, break-even point left.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis with the model.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Cash flow is more important than profit for a new business.’ Evaluate this view.
ans: For: new firms fail from running out of cash even if profitable on paper; cash pays wages/suppliers and ensures survival.
Against: without profit long-term the business is not viable; profit funds growth and attracts investors; both matter.
Judgement: in the short term/start-up phase cash is critical for survival; profit is essential for long-term viability – both needed, cash more urgent early on.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘stakeholder’.
ans: Any individual or group with an interest in / affected by the activities of a business (2).

parts.text: Identify two external stakeholders of Lumina affected by the closure decision.
ans: Any two: local community, local government, customers, suppliers, trade union (as external body), wider society.

parts.text: Explain how the closure decision conflicts with Lumina’s mission statement.
ans: Mission stresses ‘responsibly’/ethical image, but closing the town’s largest employer harms the community.
Reputation for ethics is undermined, risking customer trust (as customers warned).
1–2 link to mission + 2 development.

parts.text: Analyse the likely reactions of two stakeholder groups to the proposed closure.
ans: Employees/union: opposition, strike threat, fall in morale (70% unionised).
Shareholders: support closure for cost savings/profit but wary of reputation damage.
Local government: resistance, offers grant to protect local jobs.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two groups’ reactions analysed with the case.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies reactions, limited application.

parts.text: Using Table 1, analyse the financial case for and against closing the factory in the first year.
ans: =First-year net effect ≈ +$4.1m saving − $3.6m redundancy − $1.8m lost sales = −$1.3m (a first-year loss).
Ongoing years: saving of $4.1m − $1.8m lost sales ≈ +$2.3m/yr once one-off redundancy passes.
Staying open with the grant adds $0.9m/yr for two years but forgoes the $4.1m saving.
So closure hurts year one but may benefit later years – depends on how long reputation damage lasts.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Correct use of figures with analysis of short vs long term.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some correct calculation/analysis.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Limited use of data.

parts.text: Recommend whether Lumina should close the factory. Justify your recommendation using the case and figures.
ans: #For closing
Long-run cost savings ($4.1m), shareholder pressure, competitiveness.
#Against closing
First-year loss, 620 jobs, damage to CSR mission and customer relationships, strike disruption, community impact; grant available.
#Judgement

Supported recommendation, e.g. delay/keep open using the grant while investing to cut costs, or phased closure with retraining to protect reputation; weigh short-term loss vs long-term gain and the mission.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses data, justified recommendation with awareness of stakeholders and mission.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

12.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
12.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between piece rate and salary as payment methods.
ans: Piece rate: pay per unit produced – output-linked (2).
Salary: fixed annual pay regardless of output/hours, usually paid monthly (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one drawback of paying factory workers by piece rate.
ans: May sacrifice quality for quantity; unsuitable where output is hard to measure; income insecurity. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘mission statement’.
ans: A short statement of a business’s core purpose/reason for existing (1) that guides its overall direction and values (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the relationship between a mission statement, objectives and tactics.
ans: Mission = overall purpose; aims = broad long-term goals derived from it.
Objectives = specific measurable targets to achieve the aims (often SMART).
Strategy = long-term plan to meet objectives; tactics = short-term actions implementing the strategy.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Clear explanation of the hierarchy/links.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Defines terms with limited linkage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two consequences for a business of poor management–workforce relations.
ans: Any two: strikes/industrial action, low morale, high turnover, low productivity, poor reputation, difficulty recruiting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way managers can improve cooperation with the workforce.
ans: Consultation/participation, fair pay, good communication, recognition, involving unions. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways a business could improve low capacity utilisation.
ans: Increase demand (marketing/new markets/price cuts).
Reduce capacity (rationalise – close a line/site, sell assets).
Subcontract/produce for other firms; diversify.
#Marks
Up to 3 per method.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why high capacity utilisation reduces unit costs.
ans: Fixed costs are spread over more units, lowering fixed cost per unit and total average cost. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘corporate social responsibility (CSR)’.
ans: The idea that a business should act ethically (1) and consider the impact of its decisions on society and the environment (1), beyond legal minimums and profit (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse one benefit and one cost to a business of adopting CSR.
ans: Benefit: improved reputation/brand loyalty, staff motivation, differentiation, avoiding regulation.
Cost: higher operating costs (ethical sourcing, lower emissions) may raise prices/reduce short-term profit.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Both sides analysed with development.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies a benefit/cost, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how contribution costing can help with a special order decision.
ans: Accept an order if its price exceeds variable cost (positive contribution), since fixed costs are already covered – it adds to profit. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one situation where contribution costing should NOT be used for pricing.
ans: Long-term/all pricing (fixed costs must be covered eventually); if spare capacity is not available; risk of undercharging. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘assessment centre’.
ans: A selection method where candidates complete a series of tasks/tests/exercises over one or more days (1), observed by assessors (1), to judge their suitability (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one benefit and one drawback of using assessment centres.
ans: Benefit: broader, more reliable picture of ability. Drawback: expensive/time-consuming. 2 each developed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between cash and profit.
ans: Profit = revenue − expenses (accruals); cash = actual money in/out (timing differs) (2+2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a profitable business can run out of cash.
ans: Cash tied up in receivables/inventory or spent on assets/loan repayment while profit is only on paper. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘cash flow forecast’.
ans: An estimate of the expected cash inflows and outflows of a business (1) over a future period, showing opening/closing balances (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits of producing a cash flow forecast.
ans: Identifies potential cash shortages in advance so action can be taken (arrange overdraft).
Supports loan applications and planning; monitors performance.
Helps time spending/investment.
#Marks
Up to 3 per benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘sample’ in market research.
ans: A representative sub-group of the target population (1) selected to be surveyed instead of the whole population (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why sampling is necessary and one limitation of it.
ans: Necessary: surveying everyone is too costly/time-consuming. Limitation: risk of sampling error/unrepresentative sample -> misleading results. 2 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how Herzberg’s two-factor theory could guide a business trying to raise motivation.
ans: First remove dissatisfaction: fair pay, decent conditions, fair supervision (hygiene).
Then build motivators: responsibility, achievement, recognition, advancement (job enrichment).
Improving hygiene alone will not motivate.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether empowering employees is always beneficial for a business.
ans: For: raises motivation/ownership, faster decisions, uses staff ideas, develops skills, frees managers.
Against: some staff lack skill/desire (Theory X); risk of errors/inconsistency; managers may resist losing control; needs training and trust.
Judgement: beneficial where staff are capable and well-trained and the task suits autonomy; depends on culture and workforce. Not universal.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the costs to a business of a high level of labour turnover.
ans: Recruitment, selection and induction costs recur frequently.
Training costs and lost productivity while new staff learn.
Loss of experienced staff, knowledge, morale and customer relationships.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of several costs.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the most effective methods a business could use to reduce labour turnover.
ans: Options: better pay/benefits, improved working conditions, training/promotion, better recruitment/selection fit, motivation (job enrichment), management style.
Trade-offs: cost of higher pay vs cost of turnover; non-financial methods may be cheaper and durable.
Judgement: root cause matters – if pay is the issue address pay, if boredom then job design; a combination targeted at causes is most effective. Depends on context.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how capacity utilisation, productivity and unit costs are linked.
ans: Higher utilisation spreads fixed costs -> lower fixed cost per unit.
Higher productivity lowers variable/labour cost per unit.
Together they cut average cost and raise competitiveness/profit.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of the links.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Outsourcing always harms the workforce.’ Evaluate this statement.
ans: For: can cause redundancies, insecurity and lower morale among remaining staff.
Against: can protect the business’s survival (saving other jobs), let staff focus on higher-value core work, and create jobs at suppliers; retraining/redeployment possible.
Judgement: impact depends on scale, how it is managed and whether jobs are redeployed; not always harmful. Context-dependent.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the factors a business should consider when choosing a source of finance for expansion.
ans: Cost (interest/fees/dividends), need to retain control, use (short vs long term).
Existing gearing/level of debt, flexibility, and risk.
Match the source to the purpose.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘A business that manages its people well will succeed.’ Evaluate this view.
ans: For: motivated, skilled, well-led staff raise productivity, quality, service and innovation.
Against: also needs the right product, market, operations and finance; external factors (recession, competition) matter; good HRM is necessary but not sufficient.
Judgement: people management is a major driver but success requires all functions and a viable strategy. Depends on context.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘adverse variance’.
ans: When the actual figure is worse than budget – costs higher or revenue/profit lower than planned (2).

parts.text: Calculate the sales revenue variance and state whether it is favourable or adverse.
ans: =55,200 − 48,000 = $7,200 higher revenue -> $7,200 FAVOURABLE

parts.text: Calculate the profit variance and state its type.
ans: =16,100 − 12,000 = $4,100 higher profit -> $4,100 FAVOURABLE

parts.text: The ingredient cost variance is $2,600 adverse. Explain why this may not indicate poor performance by the manager.
ans: Sales were well above budget (+$7,200), so more customers were served -> naturally higher ingredient costs.
An incremental (fixed) budget does not flex for the higher volume, so the ‘adverse’ cost variance is largely due to extra sales, not waste.
1–2 + development.

parts.text: Analyse how using a flexible budget would give a fairer assessment of the Riverside café.
ans: A flexible budget adjusts cost targets to the actual (higher) level of sales/customers.
It separates genuine efficiency/overspending from volume-driven cost rises, so the manager is judged fairly.
Reduces demotivation and improves control accuracy.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis using the case.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.text: Recommend how Cobalt should budget for its cafés in future (e.g. incremental, flexible, zero-based, with more manager involvement). Justify your recommendation.
ans: #Weigh options

Incremental: simple but unfair for growing/variable cafés (as at Riverside). Flexible: fairer performance measure, adjusts for volume. Zero-based: controls waste but costly/time-consuming across many cafés. Participation: improves accuracy and motivation.
#Judgement

Supported recommendation, e.g. adopt flexible budgets with manager involvement so targets reflect actual customer volumes and use local knowledge, improving fairness, motivation and control; perhaps periodic zero-based reviews of overheads. Justify using Riverside’s variances.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, uses case, justified recommendation.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

13.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
13.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term ‘triple bottom line’.
ans: Measuring performance against three objectives: economic/financial profit (1), social impact (people) (1) and environmental impact (planet) (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason a business might struggle to meet all three parts of the triple bottom line.
ans: They can conflict – e.g. cutting emissions (environmental) raises costs and reduces profit (economic). 1 + 2 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the reliability of data.
ans: The extent to which data is accurate, unbiased and would give consistent results if repeated (1); influenced by sample size/method and source (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one factor that could reduce the reliability of market research data.
ans: Small/biased sample, leading questions, out-of-date secondary data, dishonest responses. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘margin of safety’.
ans: The amount by which current/actual output exceeds the break-even output (1); how far sales can fall before a loss (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the previous firm (break-even 4,000 units), calculate the margin of safety and profit if it sells 7,000 units.
ans: =Margin of safety = 7,000 − 4,000 = 3,000 units
=Profit = margin of safety × contribution = 3,000 × 15 = $45,000 (or total contribution 7,000×15=105,000 − FC 60,000 = $45,000)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘market share’.
ans: The proportion of total sales in a market (by value or volume) held by one business/product (1), usually expressed as a percentage (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A firm sells $6m in a market worth $40m. Calculate its market share and explain one implication of a rising share.
ans: =Market share = (6 / 40) × 100 = 15%
Rising share suggests growing competitiveness/brand strength, possible economies of scale and market power.
2 calc + up to 3 explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘flow production’.
ans: Continuous mass production of standardised products on a production line (1), each stage flowing to the next (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of flow production.
ans: High set-up cost, inflexible/hard to customise, breakdowns halt the whole line, repetitive/demotivating work. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Budgeted materials cost was $40,000; actual was $46,000. Calculate the variance and state whether it is favourable or adverse.
ans: =Variance = 46,000 − 40,000 = $6,000 higher cost -> $6,000 ADVERSE
2 calc + 1 favourable/adverse.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one possible cause of this variance.
ans: Higher supplier prices, more waste, higher output than planned, poor purchasing. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘induction training’.
ans: Initial training for new employees (1) to familiarise them with the job, workplace and procedures (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits of induction training to a business.
ans: New staff become productive faster and make fewer errors.
Improves safety and morale; reduces early leaving/turnover.
Communicates culture and expectations.
#Marks
Up to 3 per benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a bank loan and a bank overdraft.
ans: Loan: a fixed sum borrowed and repaid with interest over a set period (long-term) (2).
Overdraft: the ability to withdraw more than is in the account up to a limit (short-term, flexible) (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one situation where an overdraft is more suitable than a loan.
ans: Covering short-term/temporary cash shortfalls (e.g. seasonal gaps) where flexibility is needed. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘variance’.
ans: Difference between a budgeted figure and the actual figure (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Budgeted profit was $90,000; actual was $78,000. Calculate the variance and state its type.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘break-even level of output’.
ans: The level of output at which total revenue equals total costs (1), so the business makes neither profit nor loss (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A firm has fixed costs of $60,000, price $25 and variable cost $10 per unit. Calculate the break-even output.
ans: =Contribution per unit = 25 − 10 = $15
=Break-even = fixed costs / contribution = 60,000 / 15 = 4,000 units

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how the relative power of different stakeholders can affect a business decision to close a factory.
ans: Shareholders/finance providers may push for closure to cut costs (high power).
Employees/unions may resist through industrial action (power varies with unionisation).
Local community/government may exert pressure (planning, grants, reputation).
The most powerful/most affected groups shape the final decision.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of relative influence.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether pursuing CSR objectives is worthwhile for a business operating in a very competitive market.
ans: For: differentiation, customer loyalty, staff motivation, risk reduction, long-term reputation.
Against: raises costs and prices when rivals compete on price; benefits are long-term/hard to measure; may not survive short-term price war.
Judgement: depends on target market (ethical consumers?), cost structure and rivals; CSR can be a competitive advantage but must be affordable.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement, contextual.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how promoting diversity and equality could give a business a competitive advantage.
ans: Wider talent pool and creativity/innovation from varied perspectives.
Better serves diverse markets; stronger employer brand/reputation.
Improved morale/retention and legal compliance.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether on-the-job training is better than off-the-job training for a fast-food chain.
ans: On-the-job: cheap, job-specific, productive during training, immediate; but may reproduce bad habits and disrupt service.
Off-the-job: specialist skills/qualifications (e.g. management), no service distraction; but costly and less job-specific.
Judgement: for routine operational roles on-the-job usually suits a fast-food chain; off-the-job better for supervisory/management development. Depends on role and cost.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement, contextual.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the benefits to a business of cooperation between management and the workforce.
ans: Smoother change/flexibility, fewer disputes and less disruption.
Higher morale, productivity and retention; useful shop-floor ideas.
Better reputation as an employer.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Improving employee welfare is a cost the business cannot always justify.’ Evaluate this statement.
ans: For: welfare spending (facilities, benefits, wellbeing) raises costs and may not directly raise output; hard to measure returns; competitors may not.
Against: reduces absence/turnover, raises morale/productivity and reputation, aids recruitment and legal compliance – often pays for itself.
Judgement: justified where it targets real needs and improves performance/retention; depends on affordability and the labour market.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how effectiveness differs from efficiency in judging operational performance.
ans: Efficiency = resource use/cost per unit; effectiveness = meeting objectives/customer needs.
A firm can be efficient yet ineffective (wrong product) or effective yet inefficient (high cost).
Both needed for competitiveness.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis with examples.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether a small furniture maker should switch from job to batch production as demand grows.
ans: For: batch raises volume/lower unit cost, meets growing demand, some economies of scale.
Against: loses bespoke/premium appeal and flexibility, needs investment/retraining, downtime and possible redundancies, may erode USP.
Judgement: depends on whether customers value customisation or lower price, finance and demand size; perhaps a hybrid (batch for standard ranges, job for bespoke).
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement, contextual.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Calculate the contribution per pizza.
ans: =Contribution = 9.00 − 3.60 = $5.40 per pizza

parts.text: Calculate the break-even level of output per month (in pizzas).
ans: =Break-even = fixed costs / contribution = 16,200 / 5.40 = 3,000 pizzas per month
2 method + 1 answer (3,000).

DIAG|breakeven|Worked chart: TR = $9.00Q, TC = $16,200 + $3.60Q. Break-even where they cross at 3,000 pizzas (revenue = $27,000). At 4,000 pizzas the margin of safety is 1,000 pizzas and profit is $5,400.

parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety and monthly profit at the expected volume of 4,000 pizzas.
ans: =Margin of safety = 4,000 − 3,000 = 1,000 pizzas

parts.text: Complete the cash flow forecast (Table 1): calculate the net cash flow and closing balance for each month.
ans: 2 marks per month (net + closing), max 6. Own-figure rule applies.

parts.text: Advise whether Piatto should accept the special catering order of 500 pizzas at $5.00 each.
ans: =Special-order contribution = (5.00 − 3.60) × 500 = 1.40 × 500 = $700 extra contribution.
With spare capacity and fixed costs already covered, the order adds $700 profit -> accept on contribution grounds.

L|Level 1 (1-2)|Some calculation/assertion.

parts.text: Evaluate whether break-even analysis alone is a reliable basis for the owner’s decisions.
ans: #Strengths
Quick, shows break-even (3,000), margin of safety (1,000) and profit ($5,400); useful for planning and pricing.
#Weaknesses

Assumes constant $9 price and $3.60 variable cost and that all pizzas are sold; ignores demand changes, wastage, seasonality; the special order shows real pricing is more nuanced; cash timing (Table 1 shows a $1,000 low balance in Month 1) is a separate risk.

Supported judgement: break-even is a helpful guide but not sufficient alone; the owner should also use the cash flow forecast and realistic demand estimates. Not fully reliable in isolation.
