14.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
14.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the four factors of production used in operations.
ans: Land, labour, capital, enterprise (all four for 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how improving productivity can make a business more competitive.
ans: Higher output per worker/machine lowers unit costs -> lower prices or higher margins.
Can meet demand faster, fund investment, and compete on price/quality.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis linking productivity to competitiveness.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States link, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘rationalisation’.
ans: Reducing capacity/resources (e.g. closing sites or cutting lines) (1) to cut costs and raise efficiency/utilisation (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one risk of rationalising to improve capacity utilisation.
ans: May be unable to meet future demand upturns, redundancy costs/morale, loss of skills. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘labour turnover’.
ans: Percentage of the workforce leaving over a period (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse two consequences of high labour turnover.
ans: Higher recruitment/training costs; loss of experienced staff.
Disruption, lower morale and poorer customer service.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two consequences analysed.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the relationship between capacity utilisation and profitability.
ans: Higher utilisation spreads fixed costs -> lower unit costs -> higher profit per unit, provided demand exists. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons a business might deliberately keep some spare capacity.
ans: Any: cope with demand surges/seasonality, allow maintenance, flexibility for new orders, avoid overworking staff/machines. 1–2 + 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘organic (internal) growth’.
ans: Expansion of a business using its own resources (1) – e.g. more outlets, new products – rather than by merger/takeover (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages of organic growth compared with growth by takeover.
ans: Lower risk/less disruption; growth at a manageable pace.
Avoids the high cost and culture-clash problems of acquisitions.
Easier to maintain control and existing culture.
#Marks
Up to 3 per advantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘Just in Time (JIT)’.
ans: An inventory approach where materials arrive exactly when needed for production (1), minimising stock held (1) to cut holding costs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one requirement for JIT to work successfully.
ans: Reliable suppliers/frequent deliveries, good relationships, accurate demand forecasting, quality inputs. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term ‘opportunity cost’.
ans: The benefit lost / next best alternative foregone (1) when a choice is made / a scarce resource is allocated to one use (1) rather than another (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using an example, why opportunity cost is important to an entrepreneur with limited capital.
ans: Resources (capital) are finite, so every spending decision means an alternative is sacrificed (application of scarcity).
Example: spending $20,000 on a delivery van means the same funds cannot be spent on a marketing campaign that might raise sales.
#Marks
1–2 for understanding of scarcity/choice; up to 3 further marks for applied explanation with a relevant worked example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the 4Ps of the marketing mix.
ans: Product, Price, Promotion, Place (all four for 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the elements of the marketing mix must be consistent with each other.
ans: A premium product needs a high price, quality promotion and selective distribution; mismatched Ps confuse customers and waste spending. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘unique selling point (USP)’.
ans: A feature that distinguishes a product from competitors (1) and gives customers a reason to choose it (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how a strong USP can benefit a business.
ans: Differentiation reduces direct price competition -> can charge a premium.
Aids brand loyalty, promotion and market share.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of benefits.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States benefits, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two strengths of a family business.
ans: Any two: strong commitment/loyalty; long-term outlook; trust/shared values; lower agency costs; quick decision-making; reputation continuity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse one weakness a family business may face as it grows.
ans: Succession conflict / roles given by family ties not merit, limiting professional management.
Difficulty raising capital without diluting family control.
Emotional decisions/conflict can harm the business.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of a growth-related weakness.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States a weakness, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the benefits to a business of using budgets.
ans: Planning: turns objectives into financial targets and resource allocation.
Control: variance analysis highlights problems for corrective action.
Motivation and coordination across departments.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether zero-based budgeting is better than incremental budgeting.
ans: For ZBB: eliminates waste, forces justification, allocates to priorities, good in changing conditions.
Against: very time-consuming/costly, needs skill, may cause conflict; incremental is quick, simple and stable but can carry forward inefficiency.
Judgement: ZBB better where cost control/change is critical or budgets are large; incremental suits stable, small operations. Depends on context and resources.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the impact of training and development on a business.
ans: Raises productivity, quality and flexibility (multi-skilling).
Improves motivation, morale and retention (career prospects).
Supports innovation/intrapreneurship and change; but costs money and time and trained staff may leave.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of impacts.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether spending on training is always a worthwhile investment for a business.
ans: For: higher productivity/quality, motivation, retention, adaptability, fewer errors/accidents.
Against: costly, disrupts production, trained staff may be poached, benefits hard to measure, wasted if poorly targeted.
Judgement: worthwhile if training is relevant, well-targeted and staff are retained; depends on turnover, type of work and cost. Not automatically worthwhile.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a business might benefit from clearly communicating its objectives to its workforce.
ans: Improves direction/coordination and consistent decisions.
Motivates staff (goal-setting, sense of purpose, participation).
Enables measurement of performance and accountability.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘A business should always put its shareholders’ interests first.’ Evaluate this view.
ans: For: shareholders own/risk capital; profit funds investment and survival; legal duty in some regimes.
Against: ignoring employees, customers, community and environment risks reputation, regulation, poor morale and long-term decline; stakeholder approach/CSR can raise long-term value.
Judgement: depends on time horizon and ownership; balancing stakeholders often serves shareholders best in the long run.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a business might raise labour productivity.
ans: Training and better methods; investment in machinery/automation.
Motivation (financial and non-financial), better management, reduced waste/downtime.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘Mass customisation offers the best of both job and flow production.’ Evaluate this view.
ans: For: personalisation (like job) with volume/low cost (like flow) via flexible automation; customer satisfaction plus scale.
Against: requires heavy investment in flexible technology/IT, complex operations and supply chains; not suitable for all products; can raise costs/complexity.
Judgement: powerful where technology and demand for personalisation exist; not universally best. Depends on product, market and investment capacity.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘empowerment’.
ans: Giving employees the authority/autonomy to make decisions about their own work (1) without seeking approval (1).

parts.text: Identify the motivation theorist whose ideas best match Solaris’s original bonus-per-call system, and justify your choice.
ans: Taylor / scientific management (1) – pay by results, close monitoring, standardised tasks, money as the main motivator (2).

parts.text: Using Table 1, explain one benefit and one drawback of Priya’s approach.
ans: Benefit: lower turnover (12% vs 40%) and higher satisfaction (88% vs 71%)/first-call resolution.
Drawback: longer average call time (6.4 vs 5.1 min) – fewer calls handled, possible higher cost.
2 each with data.

parts.text: Analyse how Priya’s methods could be explained using Herzberg’s or Maslow’s theory.
ans: Herzberg: recognition, responsibility and achievement are motivators driving satisfaction/lower turnover.
Maslow: esteem (recognition) and self-actualisation (responsibility, teamwork = social) needs being met.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Applies a named theory to Priya’s methods.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Mentions theory, limited application.

parts.text: Analyse how the tall organisational structure (Fig 1) might affect motivation and communication at Solaris.
ans: Tall structure -> narrow spans, many layers -> slow communication and slow decisions.
Agents feel distant from management, less empowered -> lower motivation (links to 40% turnover).
Empowerment (Priya) partly offsets this by pushing decisions down.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis using the structure and case.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

Lower turnover cuts recruitment cost; higher satisfaction and first-call resolution aid retention of customers and reputation; motivation gains.
#Against / risks
Longer call times reduce volume/raise cost per call; change management and training needed; some staff/managers may resist losing the bonus.
#Judgement

Supported recommendation, e.g. roll out but redesign rewards around quality and first-call resolution rather than pure volume; pilot further/monitor cost per resolved issue; weigh the value of retention and satisfaction against call throughput.

L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

15.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
15.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between the private sector and the public sector.
ans: Private sector: owned/controlled by private individuals or shareholders, usually profit-motivated (2).
Public sector: owned/controlled by the government, usually providing public services (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one consequence of a business moving from the public to the private sector (privatisation).
ans: Greater profit motive/efficiency incentive, access to private finance, but possible job losses or higher prices. 1 mark + 2 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘employee morale’.
ans: The overall level of confidence, satisfaction and enthusiasm employees feel (1) towards their work and employer (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how low employee morale can harm a business.
ans: Lower productivity and quality; higher absenteeism and labour turnover.
Poorer customer service and reputation; more disputes.
Higher costs of recruitment/supervision.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of consequences.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States effects, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘limited liability’.
ans: Owners’ losses are limited to the amount they invested (1); personal assets are protected (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason a growing business might change from a partnership to a private limited company.
ans: Limited liability, easier to raise capital, continuity. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘price skimming’.
ans: Setting a high initial price for a new/innovative product (1) to maximise revenue from early adopters before lowering it (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why skimming might suit a new technology product.
ans: Little competition initially, early adopters pay a premium, recovers R&D quickly; price falls as rivals enter. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘supply chain management’.
ans: The management of the flow of materials, goods and information (1) from suppliers through production to the final customer (1) to improve efficiency and reliability (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse why effective supply chain management is important to a business.
ans: Ensures reliable, cost-effective supply of the right materials at the right time.
Reduces costs, lead times and stock-outs; improves quality and customer satisfaction.
Builds resilience against disruption.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of importance.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States importance, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘adding value’.
ans: The difference between the price a customer pays and the cost of the bought-in inputs/materials used to make the product (2). It reflects the extra worth created by the business (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways a smartphone manufacturer could increase the value it adds.
ans: Stronger branding/design so customers pay a premium (e.g. a recognised premium brand).
Improved features/USP (better camera, longer battery) allowing a higher price.
Lowering input costs through bulk buying without cutting price.
#Marks
1 mark identification + up to 1–2 development for each of two ways (max 5).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three types of inventory a manufacturer holds.
ans: Raw materials (1), work in progress (1) and finished goods (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to a business of holding inventory.
ans: Meets unexpected demand/avoids stock-outs and lost sales.
Allows production to continue if deliveries are late (buffer).
Enables bulk-buying discounts; smooths seasonal demand.
#Marks
Up to 3 per benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two objectives of a public-sector organisation.
ans: Any two: provide a public service, meet social needs, control costs/stay within budget, serve all citizens, wider social welfare rather than profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the objectives of a public-sector hospital differ from those of a plc.
ans: Hospital: service/welfare and access for all within budget; plc: profit/shareholder value. 1–2 each contrast, developed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘lead time’.
ans: The time between placing an order with a supplier and receiving the goods (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a longer lead time affects the re-order level.
ans: Longer lead time means stock must be re-ordered earlier/at a higher level to avoid running out before delivery. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘collective bargaining’.
ans: Negotiation over pay/conditions (1) between employers and employee representatives (a union) on behalf of a group of workers (1) to reach a collective agreement (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason a business may prefer collective bargaining to negotiating with each worker individually.
ans: More efficient (one negotiation), consistent terms, reduces individual conflict. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how the objectives of a business might change as it moves from start-up to a large plc.
ans: Start-up: survival/cash flow; growth phase: market share/expansion.
Established plc: profit maximisation/shareholder value, possibly CSR.
Objectives shift with ownership, size, competition and the economy.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether motivation or effective management is more important to business success.
ans: Motivation: raises productivity, quality, retention; but needs direction.
Management: plans, organises, controls and leads; poor management wastes a motivated workforce.
Judgement: interdependent – good management creates the conditions for motivation; neither sufficient alone. Depends on context.

L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how effective workforce planning can help a rapidly growing business.
ans: Ensures enough skilled staff are recruited/trained ahead of demand (avoids bottlenecks).
Controls labour costs and avoids over- or under-staffing.
Identifies skills gaps and training needs; supports smooth expansion.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, applied analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether external recruitment is always better than internal recruitment for senior management posts.
ans: For external: brings new ideas/skills, wider pool, avoids internal politics, needed if no internal talent.
For internal: cheaper, faster, motivating, known performer, retains culture/knowledge.
Judgement: depends on whether change or continuity is needed, availability of internal talent, cost and urgency; not always better.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the assumptions on which break-even analysis is based.
ans: Selling price constant at all output levels; variable cost per unit constant; fixed costs constant.
All output produced is sold (no inventory build-up); single product/mix.
These simplify reality and limit accuracy.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis of assumptions.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Lists assumptions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate how useful a cash flow forecast is, given that it is based on estimates.
ans: For: even estimates reveal likely shortfalls, aid planning and finance; can be updated (rolling forecast); better than no plan.
Against: inaccurate assumptions (sales, timing, costs) can mislead; unexpected events not captured; false confidence.
Judgement: useful as a flexible planning/monitoring tool if regularly revised and realistic; not a guarantee. Depends on quality of assumptions.

L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how variance analysis can improve business performance.
ans: Identifies where actual differs from plan (favourable/adverse) and by how much.
Prompts investigation of causes and corrective action.
Improves future budgeting accuracy and accountability.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the view that budgets do more harm than good because they can demotivate staff.
ans: For: unrealistic/imposed targets and blame culture demotivate; rigidity and gaming (spending to budget) waste resources.
Against: participative, realistic budgets motivate and coordinate; control and planning benefits are substantial; problems stem from misuse, not budgets themselves.
Judgement: budgets are valuable if set participatively and realistically and used to support (not blame) staff; harm arises from poor implementation.

L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.

parts.text: Define the term ‘lead time’.
ans: Time between placing an order and receiving the goods (2).

parts.text: Using Table 1, calculate the re-order level for the key component.
ans: =Re-order level = buffer + (usage during lead time) = 800 + (1,600 × 1) = 2,400 units

ans: =Buffer holding cost ≈ 800 units × $3 = $2,400 per year (accept average-stock reasoning if shown).
2 method + 1 answer.

parts.text: Explain one drawback Vela is experiencing from holding large buffer stocks.
ans: High storage costs and cash tied up (tight cash flow), plus obsolescence when designs change.
1–2 + development using the case.

parts.text: Analyse the risks to Vela of moving to a JIT system after the recent shipping delay.
ans: JIT removes the buffer that currently protects against delays -> stock-outs would halt lines (as happened) more often.
Relies on reliable, fast local suppliers; imported parts have long, uncertain lead times.
Lost output/sales and idle labour if supply fails; but frees cash and cuts storage/obsolescence.

L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.

parts.text: Recommend an inventory strategy for Vela (e.g. full JIT, more local sourcing, or larger buffers). Justify your recommendation using the case and data.
ans: #Options
Full JIT (cuts cost/cash but risky with imports); bigger buffers (secure but costly/obsolescence); hybrid with local sourcing.

Tight cash favours cutting stock; but the recent 2-week stock-out shows disruption risk; re-order level 2,400 with buffer 800 is exposed to long import lead times.

Supported recommendation, e.g. adopt a hybrid – source key/at-risk components locally with modest buffers and apply JIT to reliable, low-risk parts; keep a control system with sensible re-order levels. Balances cash pressure against stock-out risk.

L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.

16.title: Synoptic mixed-topic paper
16.theme: Questions are drawn from across the whole AS syllabus (Sections 1-5), as in the live examination - topics are deliberately not grouped together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure.
ans: Capital expenditure: spending on non-current assets used long-term (e.g. machinery) (2).
Revenue expenditure: spending on day-to-day running costs (e.g. wages, materials) (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the distinction matters for financing decisions.
ans: Capital items funded by long-term finance; revenue items by short-term/current funds – matching finance to use. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘labour turnover’.
ans: The proportion of the workforce leaving a business over a period, usually a year (1), expressed as a percentage (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula for labour turnover and calculate it for a firm where 24 of 300 staff left this year.
ans: =Labour turnover = (number leaving / average number employed) × 100
2 for formula, 2 for correct answer 8%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between primary and secondary research.
ans: Primary (field): first-hand data collected for a specific purpose, e.g. surveys, interviews (2).
Secondary (desk): existing data collected by others, e.g. government reports, internal records (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of primary research over secondary research.
ans: Specific/up-to-date and tailored to the business’s needs; not available to rivals. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what happens to inventory levels if usage suddenly rises but the re-order level is unchanged.
ans: Stock is drawn down faster and may fall below buffer/run out before the next delivery -> stock-out risk. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two costs of running out of inventory (a stock-out).
ans: Any: lost sales/revenue, dissatisfied customers, halted production, idle labour, damaged reputation. 1–2 + 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the four factors of production.
ans: Land (1/2), labour (1/2), capital (1/2) and enterprise (1/2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how a new coffee-shop combines the four factors of production to add value.
ans: Land: the retail site/premises and raw materials (coffee beans, milk).
Labour: baristas who prepare drinks and provide service.
Capital: espresso machines, furniture, till systems.
Enterprise: the owner who organises the other three and bears the risk.
Combining them transforms low-value inputs (beans + water) into a higher-value finished drink customers will pay a premium for – this is added value.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Clear analysis linking each factor to the process of adding value in the coffee-shop context.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Factors identified/described with limited link to adding value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘labour productivity’.
ans: Output per worker per period (1); a measure of how efficiently labour is used (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A factory of 20 workers produces 6,400 units a week. Calculate labour productivity and explain one way to raise it.
ans: =Labour productivity = 6,400 / 20 = 320 units per worker per week
Raise via training, better machinery/automation, motivation or improved methods.
2 calc + up to 3 explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘social enterprise’.
ans: A business that trades to achieve social/environmental objectives (1) as well as financial ones (1), typically reinvesting surpluses to further its mission (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between the objectives of a social enterprise and a plc.
ans: Social enterprise pursues a triple bottom line (social/environmental as well as profit); a plc typically prioritises shareholder profit/return. 1 + 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the term ‘budget holder’.
ans: The person/manager responsible for setting and keeping to a particular budget (1) and for explaining variances (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how budgeting helps a business allocate and control resources.
ans: Allocates funds to departments in line with objectives/priorities.
Sets spending limits; variance analysis flags overspending for control.
Coordinates activities and prevents overspending.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of allocation/control.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|States role, limited development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how outsourcing can help a business manage fluctuating demand.
ans: Extra demand can be met by subcontracting without investing in permanent capacity; scale up/down flexibly. 1–2 + development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors a business should consider before outsourcing.
ans: Any: supplier reliability/quality, cost saving, control needed, whether it is a core activity, ethics/reputation. 1–2 + 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the four categories of the Boston Matrix.
ans: Star, Question mark (problem child), Cash cow, Dog (all four for 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Analyse how the Boston Matrix can help a business manage its product portfolio.
ans: Identifies which products to invest in (stars), harvest for cash (cash cows), review (question marks) or drop (dogs).
Guides balanced portfolio and cash allocation (cash cows fund stars).
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Developed analysis of portfolio decisions.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Describes categories, limited analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the internal sources of finance a profitable, established business could use to fund growth.
ans: Retained earnings – no cost/repayment, no dilution.
Sale of unwanted/underused assets; sale and leaseback to release cash.
Better working-capital management to free cash.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: ‘A start-up should always avoid debt finance.’ Evaluate this view.
ans: For avoiding debt: start-ups have uncertain income; fixed repayments/interest strain cash; risk of insolvency; may lack collateral.
Against: debt keeps ownership/control, is often the only realistic option, can be cheaper than equity, builds credit history; microfinance/overdrafts suit small needs.
Judgement: some debt can be appropriate if repayments are affordable and used for productive assets; blanket avoidance is unwise. Depends on cash-flow certainty and cost.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse why poor working-capital management can threaten a business’s survival.
ans: Insufficient liquidity -> cannot pay wages/suppliers/loans -> loss of credit and legal action.
Overtrading (rapid growth with too little working capital) causes cash crises.
Can lead to insolvency even when profitable.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether internal or external sources of finance are better for funding a major expansion.
ans: Internal (retained profit/asset sales): no interest/repayment/dilution, but limited in size and uses up reserves.
External (loans/shares/VC): larger sums possible, but cost, repayment, control loss or gearing risk.
Judgement: large expansion usually needs external finance; best is often a mix; depends on size, ownership, gearing and cost.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse the barriers to entrepreneurship a person starting a business in a low-income country might face.
ans: Limited access to finance (few lenders, no collateral, high interest, undeveloped capital markets).
Poor infrastructure (power, transport, internet) raising costs and limiting reach.
Low skills/education base; limited managerial experience.
Bureaucracy/corruption and unstable legal or political environment; small local purchasing power.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed, contextual analysis of several barriers.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some analysis.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Lists barriers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the contribution of business enterprise to the economic development of a country.
ans: For: creates jobs and incomes, raises output/GDP, increases tax revenue, drives innovation, reduces import dependence, develops skills, can attract investment.
Against: many start-ups fail; benefits may be uneven (regional/income inequality); possible negative externalities (pollution, exploitation); informal-sector enterprise may avoid tax.
Judgement: enterprise is a significant driver of development but must be supported by education, infrastructure and stable governance to realise its potential.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement with development-context.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited two-sided.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Analyse how a business could interpret an inventory control chart to manage stock.
ans: Read maximum, re-order and buffer levels; monitor the rate of stock usage.
Identify when to re-order (at re-order level) and spot abnormal usage or delivery delays.
Adjust re-order level/quantity as lead time or demand changes.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis referencing the chart.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate whether building resilience into the supply chain is worth the extra cost.
ans: For: protects against disruption (pandemics, wars, supplier failure), avoids costly shutdowns/lost sales, protects reputation.
Against: dual-sourcing/extra stock/local suppliers raise costs and reduce JIT savings; disruptions may be rare.
Judgement: increasingly worthwhile given recent global shocks; depends on the likelihood and cost of disruption vs the cost of resilience.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced, supported judgement.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided.

parts.text: Define the term ‘private limited company (Ltd)’.
ans: A company with limited liability whose shares are not traded publicly/are transferred privately (2).

parts.text: Identify the type of integration involved if GreenRoots takes over FarmFresh, and justify your answer.
ans: Horizontal integration (1) – both operate at the same stage of the same industry (organic food delivery) (2).

parts.text: Using Table 1, explain one reason GreenRoots might be attractive to a stock-market investor compared with FarmFresh.
ans: Higher net profit margin (7% vs 3%) indicates stronger profitability/efficiency.
Larger revenue and wider coverage suggest a stronger, more scalable business.
1–2 use of data + 2 explanation.

parts.text: Analyse two benefits to GreenRoots of the joint venture (Option 2) rather than the takeover (Option 1).
ans: Shares costs/risk of national expansion with a large, resourced partner.
Access to the supermarket’s customers, logistics and brand – faster reach.
Retains independence; avoids buying FarmFresh’s ageing vehicles/low margins.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Two benefits analysed using the case.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|Identifies benefits, limited application.

parts.text: Analyse the likely impact on GreenRoots’ stakeholders if it becomes a plc.
ans: Directors/owners: raise capital and gain status but dilute control and risk takeover.
Employees: growth may bring jobs/opportunities but also restructuring pressure.
Customers: possible price/quality changes from shareholder pressure for profit.
New shareholders: gain influence and returns but bear market risk.
L|Level 3 (6-8)|Developed analysis across stakeholders, applied.
L|Level 2 (3-5)|Some analysis.
L|Level 1 (1-2)|Identifies stakeholders.

parts.text: Recommend which growth option (takeover, joint venture, or plc flotation) GreenRoots should pursue to achieve national expansion. Justify your recommendation.
ans: #Weigh each option
Takeover: quick northern coverage but low-margin target and old assets; integration risk.
Joint venture: fast national reach, shared risk, but shared profit and possible loss of brand identity/dependence on the supermarket.
Flotation: large capital and continued control of strategy but loss of ownership control, cost and regulation.
#Judgement

Supported choice using data (e.g. JV to reach national scale quickly while directors retain ownership, then float later); recognise the objective is national expansion within three years and the owners’ wish to keep control.
L|Level 4 (10-12)|Balanced comparison, uses data, justified recommendation.
L|Level 3 (7-9)|Balanced, some judgement/application.
L|Level 2 (4-6)|Limited.
L|Level 1 (1-3)|One-sided/assertion.

B1.title: Enterprise (Syllabus 1.1)
B1.theme: Knowledge recall: nature of business activity, entrepreneurs & intrapreneurs, business plans.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘business activity’.
ans: Using resources/factors of production (1) to produce goods and services to satisfy customers’ needs and wants (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the main purpose of business activity.
ans: To combine inputs to produce output that satisfies needs/wants (1) and adds value / earns a profit or return (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘consumer goods’.
ans: Goods bought by households for personal use/final consumption (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define a ‘need’.
ans: Something essential for survival, e.g. food, water, shelter (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define a ‘want’.
ans: Something desired but not essential (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Distinguish between goods and services.
ans: Goods are tangible/physical products (1); services are intangible actions/benefits (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the four factors of production.
ans: Land, labour, capital and enterprise (all four = 2; two/three = 1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘land’ as a factor of production.
ans: All natural resources used in production (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘capital’ as a factor of production.
ans: Man-made resources/equipment used to produce goods and services (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘labour’ as a factor of production.
ans: The human/physical and mental effort used in production (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘enterprise’ as a factor of production.
ans: The willingness/ability to organise the other factors (1) and take the risk of production for profit (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the reward earned by each factor of production.
ans: Land = rent; labour = wages; capital = interest; enterprise = profit (all four = 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘adding value’.
ans: The difference between the price a customer pays (1) and the cost of bought-in inputs/materials (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula for added value.
ans: Added value = selling price − cost of bought-in materials/inputs (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify two ways a business can add value.
ans: Any two: branding, better design/features, USP, convenience, quality, customer service, packaging (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘scarcity’.
ans: Resources are finite/limited (1) but wants are unlimited (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘opportunity cost’.
ans: The next best alternative foregone (1) when a choice is made/resources allocated (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why choice is necessary for a business.
ans: Because resources are scarce, so not all wants/uses can be satisfied at once (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘economic activity’.
ans: The use of scarce resources to produce goods/services (1) to satisfy needs and wants (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain ‘the problem of choice’.
ans: Because resources are scarce (1), choosing one use means giving up another (opportunity cost) (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of opportunity cost for a business.
ans: e.g. spending on a new van means not spending on marketing (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the ‘dynamic business environment’.
ans: The business environment is constantly changing (1) – in technology, competition, tastes, laws and the economy (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors that make the business environment dynamic.
ans: Any two: technology, competition, consumer tastes, legislation, economic conditions, globalisation (1 each).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify one opportunity that change can create.
ans: Any: new products/markets, e-commerce, first-mover advantage (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why businesses succeed.
ans: Any two: good management, meeting customer needs, sound finance/cash flow, USP, innovation, motivated staff (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why businesses fail.
ans: Any two: poor cash flow/liquidity, poor management, lack of demand/market research, over-expansion, strong competition, external shocks (1 each).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the most common cause of failure for new firms.
ans: Poor cash flow / running out of cash (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a local and a national business.
ans: Local: operates in a small/single area (1); national: operates across the whole country (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define an ‘international business’.
ans: A business that trades (exports/imports) in more than one country (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define a ‘multinational business’.
ans: A business with production/operating facilities (1) in more than one country (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘entrepreneur’.
ans: A person who sets up a business (1), organising the factors of production and taking the risk for profit (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three qualities of a successful entrepreneur.
ans: Any three: risk-taking, innovation/creativity, determination, self-confidence, leadership, multi-tasking, hard work (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘intrapreneur’.
ans: An employee within a business (1) who behaves entrepreneurially – innovating using company resources (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two qualities an intrapreneur needs.
ans: Any two: creativity, initiative, willingness to take (calculated) risk, drive, problem-solving (1 each).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Distinguish between an entrepreneur and an intrapreneur.
ans: Entrepreneur bears personal financial risk starting their own business (1); intrapreneur innovates inside an existing firm without personal financial risk (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘entrepreneurship’.
ans: The activity of setting up and running a business (1), taking on financial risk in the hope of profit (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two roles of entrepreneurship in starting up a business.
ans: Any two: spotting an opportunity, raising finance, organising resources, bearing risk, making key decisions (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘intrapreneurship’.
ans: Employees acting entrepreneurially within a business (1) to develop new products/processes using company resources (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways intrapreneurship helps an established business.
ans: Any two: new products/innovation, keeps firm competitive, motivates staff, avoids complacency (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three barriers to entrepreneurship.
ans: Any three: lack of finance, lack of skills/experience, competition, fear of failure, red tape/regulation, no viable idea, limited market access (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one source of help available to entrepreneurs.
ans: Any: government grants, bank loans, business advisers/incubators, mentors, microfinance (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between risk and uncertainty.
ans: Risk: outcome is identifiable and probability can be estimated/insured (1); uncertainty: unpredictable events that cannot be foreseen/measured (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a business risk.
ans: Any: a new product not selling, machine breakdown, bad debts (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of uncertainty.
ans: Any: a pandemic, sudden change in law, natural disaster, war (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways business enterprise contributes to a country’s development.
ans: Any three: creates jobs, raises incomes/GDP, increases tax revenue, drives innovation, reduces imports, develops skills (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one negative effect enterprise can have on a country.
ans: Any: pollution/negative externalities, inequality, exploitation, tax avoidance (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘business plan’.
ans: A written document (1) setting out a business idea, objectives and how they will be achieved (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the main purpose of a business plan.
ans: To plan the venture and reduce risk (1) and to help raise finance from lenders/investors (1).

parts.text: State four key elements typically found in a business plan.
ans: Any four: executive summary, business idea/objectives, market research, marketing plan, operations plan, management/personnel, financial forecasts (cash flow/costs), sources of finance (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two benefits of writing a business plan.
ans: Any two: helps secure finance, clarifies objectives, identifies risks, acts as a benchmark/control (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of a business plan.
ans: Any two: forecasts are only estimates/may be inaccurate, time-consuming, quickly out of date, no guarantee of success (1 each).

B2.title: Business structure & size (Syllabus 1.2 & 1.3)
B2.theme: Knowledge recall: economic sectors, types of business ownership, liability, measuring size, small & family businesses, and business growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the ‘primary sector’.
ans: Extraction of natural resources, e.g. farming, mining, fishing (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the ‘secondary sector’.
ans: Manufacturing/processing of raw materials into goods (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define the ‘tertiary sector’.
ans: Provision of services, e.g. retail, banking, transport (1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Define the ‘quaternary sector’.
ans: Knowledge/information-based services, e.g. R&D, ICT, consultancy (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between the private and public sectors.
ans: Private: owned by individuals/shareholders, usually profit-motivated (1); public: owned by government, providing public services (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘privatisation’.
ans: Transfer of a business from the public to the private sector (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason the tertiary sector grows as economies develop.
ans: Rising incomes raise demand for services / de-industrialisation (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘sole trader’.
ans: A business owned and controlled by one person (1) with unlimited liability (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages of being a sole trader.
ans: Any two: easy/cheap to set up, full control, keep all profit, privacy (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘partnership’.
ans: A business owned by two or more people (1) who share responsibility, profits and (usually) unlimited liability (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of a partnership.
ans: Advantage: more capital/shared workload/skills (1); disadvantage: shared/unlimited liability, disputes, profit shared (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘unlimited liability’.
ans: Owners are personally responsible for all business debts (1); personal assets are at risk (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘limited liability’.
ans: Owners’ losses are limited to the amount invested (1); personal assets are protected (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘private limited company (Ltd)’.
ans: A company with limited liability (1) whose shares are not sold to the public/traded on a stock exchange (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of a private limited company.
ans: Any two: separate legal identity, limited liability, shares transferred privately, must file accounts (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘public limited company (plc)’.
ans: A company with limited liability (1) whose shares can be sold to the public/traded on a stock exchange (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of being a plc.
ans: Advantage: raise large capital, status (1); disadvantage: loss of control/takeover risk, regulation/disclosure (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘franchise’.
ans: An arrangement where a franchisee buys the right (1) to use an established business’s name and format for a fee/royalty (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the person who buys a franchise and the person who sells it.
ans: Buyer = franchisee (1); seller/owner of the brand = franchisor (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘co-operative’.
ans: A business owned and run by its members (1) who share the profits/benefits and decision-making (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘joint venture’.
ans: Two or more businesses (1) combining resources for a specific project while remaining separate (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘social enterprise’.
ans: A business that trades to achieve social/environmental aims (1) as well as financial ones, reinvesting surpluses (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the three objectives of the triple bottom line.
ans: Economic/financial (profit), social (people) and environmental (planet) (1 each).

parts.text: State four methods of measuring the size of a business.
ans: Any four: number of employees, revenue/turnover, capital employed, market share, market capitalisation, value of output (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of being a small business.
ans: Any two: flexible, personal service, close customer relationships, niche focus, quick decisions (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of being a small business.
ans: Any two: limited finance, few economies of scale, higher costs, vulnerable to competition, key-person risk (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two strengths of a family business.
ans: Any two: commitment/loyalty, long-term view, trust/shared values, quick decisions (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two weaknesses of a family business.
ans: Any two: succession conflict, roles by ties not merit, difficulty raising capital, emotional decisions (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘organic (internal) growth’.
ans: Expansion using a business’s own resources (1), e.g. more outlets/new products, rather than by merger/takeover (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘external growth’.
ans: Growth through merger with or takeover of another business (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a merger and a takeover.
ans: Merger: two firms agree to combine into one (1); takeover: one firm acquires control of another (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between a friendly merger and a hostile takeover.
ans: Friendly: agreed by both boards (1); hostile: target’s board opposes the acquisition (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘horizontal integration’.
ans: Merger/takeover of a firm at the same stage of the same industry (1), e.g. two supermarkets (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘conglomerate (diversifying) integration’.
ans: Merger/takeover of a firm in an unrelated industry (1) to spread risk/diversify (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘backward vertical integration’.
ans: Merger/takeover of a supplier (1) – a firm at an earlier stage of the supply chain (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘forward vertical integration’.
ans: Merger/takeover of a customer/distributor (1) – a firm at a later stage of the supply chain (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two possible benefits of a merger or takeover.
ans: Any two: economies of scale, larger market share, synergy, faster growth, reduced competition (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason a takeover may fail to achieve its objectives.
ans: Any: culture clash, overpayment, integration problems, diseconomies, loss of key staff (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘strategic alliance’.
ans: An agreement between businesses to cooperate/share resources (1) for mutual benefit while staying independent (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one difference between a joint venture and a strategic alliance.
ans: A joint venture usually creates a separate shared entity (1); an alliance is looser cooperation without a new company (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of changing from a partnership to a private limited company.
ans: Advantage: limited liability/easier to raise capital (1); disadvantage: more admin/must publish accounts, less privacy (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of small businesses in the industrial structure of some industries.
ans: Act as suppliers/subcontractors to large firms (1) and serve niche markets large firms ignore (1).

B3.title: Business objectives & stakeholders (Syllabus 1.4 & 1.5)
B3.theme: Knowledge recall: objectives in the private/public sectors, CSR, the mission–tactics hierarchy, decision-making, SMART, ethics and stakeholders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘business objective’.
ans: A specific, measurable goal (1) that a business aims to achieve within a time period (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two common objectives of a private-sector business.
ans: Any two: survival, profit maximisation, growth, market share, shareholder value (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two objectives of a public-sector organisation.
ans: Any two: provide a public service, meet social needs, stay within budget, serve all citizens (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one objective specific to a social enterprise.
ans: A social/environmental aim, e.g. reducing poverty or emissions (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why objectives are important to a business.
ans: Give direction, aid decision-making, motivate and allow performance to be measured (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘corporate social responsibility (CSR)’.
ans: A business acting ethically (1) and considering its impact on society and the environment beyond profit/law (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two examples of CSR in practice.
ans: Any two: fair wages, ethical sourcing, reducing pollution, community projects, recycling (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘mission statement’.
ans: A short statement of a business’s core purpose/reason for existing (1) that guides its direction and values (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘aims’.
ans: Broad, long-term goals of the business (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘strategy’.
ans: A long-term plan (1) to achieve the business’s objectives (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘tactics’.
ans: Short-term actions/decisions (1) used to implement the strategy (1).

parts.text: Place these in order from broadest to most specific: objectives, mission, tactics, aims, strategy.
ans: Mission -> aims -> objectives -> strategy -> tactics (4 marks for full correct order; 2 for mostly correct).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what each letter of ‘SMART’ objectives stands for.
ans: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-limited (all five = 3; 3–4 = 2; 1–2 = 1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit of setting SMART objectives.
ans: Any: clear focus, measurable progress, motivation, easier control (1).

parts.text: State the stages of business decision-making, in order.
ans: Set objectives -> gather data/information -> analyse options -> make/choose decision -> implement -> review/evaluate (4 for logical full sequence).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘business ethics’.
ans: Moral principles/values (1) that guide how a business behaves and makes decisions (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way ethics might influence a business objective.
ans: e.g. an objective to use only fair-trade suppliers or cut emissions (1), possibly sacrificing some profit (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons a business’s objectives might change over time.
ans: Any two: change in size/stage, economic conditions, new ownership, competition, CSR pressure (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how objectives are translated into departmental action.
ans: Through targets and budgets (1) set for departments/individuals (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘stakeholder’.
ans: Any individual or group (1) with an interest in, or affected by, the activities of a business (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between internal and external stakeholders.
ans: Internal: within the business (owners, managers, employees) (1); external: outside it (customers, suppliers, government, community) (1).

parts.text: Identify whether each is internal or external: (i) employees, (ii) suppliers, (iii) shareholders, (iv) local community.
ans: (i) internal; (ii) external; (iii) internal; (iv) external (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two internal stakeholders of a business.
ans: Any two: owners/shareholders, managers, employees (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two external stakeholders of a business.
ans: Any two: customers, suppliers, government, local community, lenders, pressure groups (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one aim of shareholders as stakeholders.
ans: High profit/dividends and rising share value (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one aim of employees as stakeholders.
ans: Fair pay, job security, good conditions (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one aim of customers as stakeholders.
ans: Good quality, fair prices, good service (1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one aim of the local community as a stakeholder.
ans: Jobs, low pollution/nuisance, community support (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two rights of employees as stakeholders.
ans: Any two: fair pay, safe conditions, a contract, non-discrimination, consultation (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one responsibility of employees.
ans: Any: work diligently, follow rules, act honestly/safely (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘stakeholder conflict’.
ans: When the aims of different stakeholder groups clash (1) so satisfying one harms another (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of stakeholder conflict.
ans: e.g. shareholders want higher profit via cost-cutting, but employees want higher pay/security (2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a business being ‘accountable’ to stakeholders.
ans: Being answerable/responsible to stakeholders (1) for the effects of its decisions/actions (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason a business needs to be accountable to stakeholders.
ans: Any: builds trust, meets legal/ethical duty, protects reputation, reduces conflict (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘profit maximisation’.
ans: Aiming to make the greatest possible profit (1) – the largest gap between total revenue and total cost (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a start-up may focus on survival rather than profit.
ans: Early cash flow is fragile and demand uncertain (1), so staying solvent matters most first (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways communicating objectives can affect the workforce.
ans: Any two: increases motivation/focus, sense of purpose, coordination, or pressure if unrealistic (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one impact of changing objectives on stakeholders.
ans: e.g. a growth objective may bring jobs for employees (1) but risk for shareholders or disruption for the community (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘budget’ in the context of objectives.
ans: A financial plan/target (1) that allocates resources to help achieve objectives (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the link between corporate and functional objectives.
ans: Functional (departmental) objectives are derived from (1) and support the overall corporate objectives (1).

B4.title: Human resource management (Syllabus 2.1)
B4.theme: Knowledge recall: HRM roles, workforce planning, labour turnover, recruitment & selection, redundancy/dismissal, morale, training, and workforce relations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘human resource management (HRM)’.
ans: Managing the recruitment, development, deployment and welfare of employees (1) to meet organisational objectives (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two roles of HRM.
ans: Any two: workforce planning, recruitment/selection, training, managing relations/morale, appraisal, dismissal/redundancy (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘workforce plan’.
ans: A plan forecasting the number and type of employees needed (1) and how to obtain/retain them (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors considered in workforce planning.
ans: Any two: forecast demand/growth, labour turnover, retirements, skills needed, technology, budget (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘labour turnover’.
ans: The percentage of the workforce that leaves (1) over a period, usually a year (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula for labour turnover.
ans: (Number of staff leaving / average number employed) × 100 (2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two implications of high labour turnover.
ans: Any two: higher recruitment/training costs, loss of experience, disruption, low morale (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one implication of very low labour turnover.
ans: Few new ideas/skills, ageing workforce, harder to reduce staff numbers (1–2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a job description and a person specification.
ans: Job description: the duties/tasks of the role (1); person specification: the skills/qualities the candidate needs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two methods of advertising a vacancy.
ans: Any two: job advertisement, employment agency, online recruitment, internal notice (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between internal and external recruitment.
ans: Internal: filling a post with an existing employee (1); external: recruiting from outside the business (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of internal recruitment.
ans: Cheaper/faster, known candidate, motivating (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage of external recruitment.
ans: New ideas/skills, wider pool (1).

parts.text: State four methods of selecting employees.
ans: Any four: CV/résumé, application form, interview, references, testing, assessment centre (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘assessment centre’.
ans: A selection method where candidates complete tasks/tests (1) observed by assessors to judge suitability (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of interviews.
ans: Advantage: face-to-face assessment (1); disadvantage: subjective/biased (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘employment contract’.
ans: A legal agreement between employer and employee (1) setting out terms such as pay, hours and duties (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items usually included in an employment contract.
ans: Any two: pay, hours, holiday, notice period, job title/duties (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between redundancy and dismissal.
ans: Redundancy: the job is no longer needed – not the employee’s fault (1); dismissal: employment ended due to the employee’s conduct/capability (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between voluntary and involuntary redundancy.
ans: Voluntary: the employee chooses to leave (often for a payment) (1); involuntary: the employer selects who must go (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘unfair dismissal’.
ans: Ending employment without a fair reason (1) or without following a fair procedure (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a fair reason for dismissal.
ans: Any: gross misconduct, poor performance/capability, theft (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘employee morale’.
ans: The confidence, satisfaction and enthusiasm (1) employees feel towards their work/employer (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two signs of low morale.
ans: Any two: high absenteeism, high labour turnover, low productivity, disputes (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘work–life balance’.
ans: The balance between time/effort spent on work and on personal/family life (1) affecting wellbeing (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways to improve employees’ work–life balance.
ans: Any two: flexible/remote working, part-time/job share, generous leave, limiting overtime (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘diversity’ in the workplace.
ans: Employing people from a wide range of backgrounds (1) and valuing their differences (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit of workplace diversity.
ans: Any: wider talent pool, creativity, understanding of diverse customers, reputation (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘induction training’.
ans: Training given to new employees when they join (1) to introduce them to the job, workplace and procedures (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between on-the-job and off-the-job training.
ans: On-the-job: training at the workplace while doing the job (1); off-the-job: training away from the normal workplace (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one advantage of on-the-job training.
ans: Cheap, job-specific, productive while training (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of off-the-job training.
ans: Specialist expertise/qualifications, fewer distractions (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one drawback of training for a business.
ans: Cost, time/disruption, trained staff may leave (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘multi-skilling’.
ans: Training employees to perform several tasks/roles (1) to increase workforce flexibility (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘employee development’.
ans: The long-term growth of employees’ skills, knowledge and careers (1) beyond immediate job training (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘trade union’.
ans: An organisation of workers (1) that represents and protects their collective interests (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘collective bargaining’.
ans: Negotiation of pay/conditions (1) between an employer and a union on behalf of a group of workers (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one benefit to employees of trade union membership.
ans: Collective bargaining power, representation in disputes (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit to an employer of dealing with a union.
ans: Single negotiation channel, fewer individual disputes, efficient communication (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one consequence of poor management–workforce relations.
ans: Strikes, low morale, high turnover, low productivity (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways cooperation between management and workforce benefits a business.
ans: Any two: smoother change, fewer disputes, higher morale/productivity, useful ideas (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how employee development can encourage intrapreneurship.
ans: Builds skills and confidence (1) so staff generate and pursue new ideas within the firm (1).

B5.title: Motivation & management (Syllabus 2.2 & 2.3)
B5.theme: Knowledge recall: motivation theories (Taylor, Mayo, Maslow, Herzberg, McClelland, Vroom), financial & non-financial motivators, management functions and styles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘motivation’.
ans: The internal drive/desire (1) that causes people to act to achieve a goal/work well (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits to a business of a motivated workforce.
ans: Any two: higher productivity/quality, lower absenteeism/turnover, better service, more ideas (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline Taylor’s theory of motivation.
ans: Scientific management: workers motivated mainly by money (1); find the most efficient method (1) and pay by results/piece rate with close control (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one criticism of Taylor’s approach.
ans: Ignores social/psychological needs; treats workers as machines (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the main finding of Mayo’s Hawthorne studies.
ans: Workers are motivated by social factors/group belonging and attention (1); productivity rose when they felt valued/consulted (1) – the human relations school (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way to apply Mayo’s ideas.
ans: Teamwork, consulting/involving staff, showing interest (1).

parts.text: List the five levels of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, lowest to highest.
ans: Physiological -> safety/security -> social/belonging -> esteem -> self-actualisation (4 for full correct order; 2 if minor errors).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one workplace example of a ‘physiological’ need being met.
ans: Pay/wages, breaks, rest facilities (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one workplace example of an ‘esteem’ need being met.
ans: Recognition, status, promotion (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one workplace example of a ‘self-actualisation’ need being met.
ans: Challenging work, development, achieving potential (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between Herzberg’s motivators and hygiene factors.
ans: Motivators (e.g. achievement, recognition) cause satisfaction (1); hygiene factors (e.g. pay, conditions) cause dissatisfaction if poor but do not motivate (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of hygiene factors.
ans: Any two: pay, working conditions, supervision, company policy, job security (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State McClelland’s three needs.
ans: Need for achievement, need for affiliation, need for power (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one implication of McClelland’s theory for managers.
ans: Match roles/rewards to an individual’s dominant need (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three components of Vroom’s expectancy theory.
ans: Expectancy, instrumentality and valence (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what ‘valence’ means.
ans: The value/importance the individual places on the reward (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘job enrichment’.
ans: Redesigning a job to add more challenging, meaningful tasks and responsibility (1) to increase motivation (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between job enrichment and job enlargement.
ans: Enrichment: adds more responsibility/depth (vertical) (1); enlargement: adds more tasks of similar level (horizontal) (1).

parts.text: State four financial methods of payment/reward.
ans: Any four: time rate, salary, piece rate, commission, bonus, profit sharing, performance-related pay, fringe benefits (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between piece rate and time rate.
ans: Piece rate: pay per unit produced (1); time rate: pay per hour/time worked (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘commission’.
ans: Pay based on a percentage of sales made (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘fringe benefits’.
ans: Non-cash rewards, e.g. company car, health insurance (1).

parts.text: State four non-financial methods of motivation.
ans: Any four: job enrichment, job rotation, teamwork, empowerment, participation, training, promotion, status, job redesign (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘empowerment’.
ans: Giving employees authority/autonomy (1) to make decisions about their own work (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘delegation’.
ans: Passing authority for a task down to a subordinate (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way employees can participate in management.
ans: Works councils, quality circles, worker directors, team meetings (1).

parts.text: State the four functions of management identified by Fayol.
ans: Planning, organising, directing (commanding), controlling (coordinating accepted) (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three categories of management roles identified by Mintzberg.
ans: Interpersonal, informational and decisional roles (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of an interpersonal role.
ans: Figurehead, leader or liaison (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘autocratic’ management style.
ans: The manager makes decisions alone and directs staff (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘democratic’ management style.
ans: The manager consults and involves staff in decisions (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘laissez-faire’ management style.
ans: The manager gives staff freedom to make their own decisions with little direction (1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Define ‘paternalistic’ management style.
ans: The manager makes decisions but explains them and considers staff welfare (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline McGregor’s Theory X view of workers.
ans: Assumes workers dislike work, avoid responsibility (1) and must be controlled/directed and motivated by money (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline McGregor’s Theory Y view of workers.
ans: Assumes workers enjoy work, seek responsibility (1) and are self-motivated and creative (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one situation where an autocratic style is suitable.
ans: A crisis/emergency or with unskilled/new staff (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one situation where a laissez-faire style is suitable.
ans: With highly skilled/creative/self-motivated staff (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one benefit of a democratic style.
ans: Higher motivation, better ideas, buy-in (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘leadership’.
ans: The ability to influence/inspire others (1) towards achieving goals (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one difference between a manager and a leader.
ans: Managers plan/organise/control tasks (1); leaders inspire, set vision and motivate people (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways a manager contributes to business performance.
ans: Any two: sets direction, allocates resources, motivates staff, controls/monitors, solves problems (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit of using financial and non-financial motivators together.
ans: Meets both economic and psychological needs (1), giving stronger, more lasting motivation (1).

B6.title: Nature of marketing & market research (Syllabus 3.1 & 3.2)
B6.theme: Knowledge recall: marketing objectives, demand & supply, markets, mass/niche, segmentation, CRM and market research.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘marketing’.
ans: The process of identifying and satisfying customer needs (1) profitably (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘marketing objective’.
ans: A specific marketing goal, e.g. to raise market share or brand awareness (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the link between marketing and corporate objectives.
ans: Marketing objectives are derived from and support corporate objectives (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two factors that influence demand for a product.
ans: Any two: price, income, price of substitutes/complements, tastes, advertising, season (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors that influence supply of a product.
ans: Any two: costs of production, technology, number of suppliers, weather (for agriculture), taxes (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘equilibrium price’.
ans: The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied (1) – the market clears (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to price if demand rises while supply is unchanged.
ans: Price rises (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to price if supply rises while demand is unchanged.
ans: Price falls (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a consumer market and an industrial market.
ans: Consumer (B2C): sold to households for personal use (1); industrial (B2B): sold to other businesses for production (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what B2C and B2B stand for.
ans: B2C = business to consumer (1); B2B = business to business (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between product orientation and market orientation.
ans: Product-orientated: focuses on the product/what the firm can make (1); market-orientated: focuses on customer needs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one risk of being product-orientated.
ans: May produce goods customers do not want (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one benefit of being market-orientated.
ans: Products match customer needs, higher sales/loyalty (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘market share’.
ans: The proportion of total sales in a market (1) held by one business/product, as a percentage (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula for market share.
ans: (Business sales / total market sales) × 100 (2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘market growth’.
ans: The increase in the total size/sales of a market (1) over a period, as a percentage (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one implication of a rising market share.
ans: Growing competitiveness/brand strength, more market power (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between mass marketing and niche marketing.
ans: Mass: aiming at the whole/large market with a standard offer (1); niche: targeting a small specific segment (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of niche marketing.
ans: Less competition, premium prices, close customer relations (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage of mass marketing.
ans: High volume, economies of scale, wide reach (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘market segmentation’.
ans: Dividing a market into distinct groups (1) with similar characteristics/needs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the three main methods of segmentation.
ans: Geographic, demographic and psychographic (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one example of demographic segmentation.
ans: Age, gender, income, occupation, family size (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of geographic segmentation.
ans: Region, country, urban/rural, climate (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of psychographic segmentation.
ans: Lifestyle, values, personality, attitudes (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one advantage of market segmentation.
ans: Precise targeting, tailored offers, less waste (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage of market segmentation.
ans: Research cost, may miss customers, smaller volumes per segment (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘target market’.
ans: The specific group of customers a business aims its product at (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘customer relationship marketing (CRM)’.
ans: A strategy focused on building long-term relationships with customers (1) to increase loyalty and repeat purchases (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit and one cost of CRM.
ans: Benefit: loyalty/repeat sales/higher lifetime value (1); cost: CRM systems/staff time/data management (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘market research’.
ans: The systematic gathering and analysis of data (1) about customers, competitors and the market (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two purposes of market research.
ans: Any two: identify customer needs, size/growth of market, competitors, test the marketing mix, reduce risk (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between primary and secondary research.
ans: Primary (field): first-hand data collected for a specific purpose (1); secondary (desk): existing data collected by others (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of primary research.
ans: Specific, current, exclusive/tailored (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage of secondary research.
ans: Cheap, quick, good for market size/trends (1).

parts.text: State four methods of primary research.
ans: Any four: questionnaire/survey, interview, focus group, observation, test marketing (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two sources of secondary research.
ans: Any two: government statistics, market reports, internet, internal sales records, trade journals (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one limitation of secondary data.
ans: May be out of date, general, or available to competitors (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘sample’.
ans: A representative sub-group of the target population (1) selected for research instead of everyone (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason sampling is necessary.
ans: Surveying everyone is too costly/time-consuming (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one limitation of sampling.
ans: Risk of sampling error/unrepresentative sample (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between quantitative and qualitative data.
ans: Quantitative: numerical/measurable data (1); qualitative: opinions/attitudes/reasons, descriptive (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason a business uses both types.
ans: Quantitative shows how many/how much (1); qualitative explains why (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the ‘reliability’ of data.
ans: The extent to which data is accurate/unbiased (1) and would give consistent results if repeated (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one factor that reduces reliability of research data.
ans: Small/biased sample, leading questions, out-of-date data, dishonest answers (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways data can be presented visually.
ans: Any two: bar chart, pie chart, line graph, table, pictogram (1 each).
