parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit of presenting data in charts.
ans: Easier to interpret/compare, spot trends quickly (1).

B7.title: The marketing mix (Syllabus 3.3)
B7.theme: Knowledge recall: the 4Ps, product & product portfolio (PLC, Boston Matrix), pricing methods, promotion, branding, packaging and place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the 4Ps of the marketing mix.
ans: Product, Price, Promotion, Place (all four = 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the elements of the marketing mix must be consistent.
ans: A premium product needs a high price, quality promotion and selective distribution (1); mismatched Ps confuse customers/waste spend (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a good and a service.
ans: A good is a tangible physical product (1); a service is intangible (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between tangible and intangible product attributes.
ans: Tangible: physical features (size, materials) (1); intangible: image, brand, service/reputation (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘unique selling point (USP)’.
ans: A feature that distinguishes a product from competitors (1) and gives customers a reason to choose it (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘product differentiation’.
ans: Making a product distinct from rivals through design, features or branding (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one benefit of product development.
ans: Keeps products competitive/extends life cycle, supports growth (1).

parts.text: State the stages of the product life cycle, in order.
ans: Development -> introduction -> growth -> maturity -> decline (4 for full correct order).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘extension strategy’.
ans: Actions to prolong the maturity stage/life of a product (1) and delay decline (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two extension strategies.
ans: Any two: new uses/markets, restyling/new features, new packaging, more promotion, price change (1 each).

parts.text: State the four categories of the Boston Matrix.
ans: Star, Question mark (problem child), Cash cow, Dog (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a ‘cash cow’.
ans: High market share (1) in a low-growth market – generates strong cash (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a ‘star’.
ans: High market share (1) in a high-growth market (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a ‘question mark’ (problem child).
ans: Low market share (1) in a high-growth market (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a ‘dog’.
ans: Low market share (1) in a low-growth market (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘penetration pricing’.
ans: Setting a low initial price (1) to enter a market/gain share quickly (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘price skimming’.
ans: Setting a high initial price for a new/innovative product (1) to maximise revenue from early adopters (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘cost-based (cost-plus) pricing’.
ans: Setting price by adding a mark-up/profit margin (1) to the unit cost (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘competitive pricing’.
ans: Setting price in line with/relative to competitors (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘psychological pricing’.
ans: Pricing to seem lower/more attractive, e.g. $9.99 (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘price discrimination’.
ans: Charging different customers different prices for the same product (1) based on willingness/ability to pay (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘dynamic pricing’.
ans: Adjusting prices in real time (1) in response to demand/timing/data, e.g. airlines (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two objectives of promotion.
ans: Any two: inform, persuade, remind, build brand/loyalty, increase sales (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between above-the-line and below-the-line promotion.
ans: Above-the-line: paid mass media advertising (1); below-the-line: targeted methods the firm controls (sales promotion, direct) (1).

parts.text: State four methods of promotion.
ans: Any four: advertising, sales promotion, direct promotion, digital/social media, public relations, personal selling (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two examples of sales promotion.
ans: Any two: discounts, BOGOF, coupons, loyalty points, free samples, competitions (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one example of a digital promotion method.
ans: Social media ads, email marketing, influencer marketing, SEO, pay-per-click (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one benefit of digital promotion.
ans: Cheap, targeted, wide reach, measurable, interactive (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one drawback of digital promotion.
ans: Ad-blocking, oversupply of ads, reputation risk, needs skills (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one benefit of traditional advertising (e.g. TV).
ans: Wide/mass reach, builds brand, high trust (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘branding’.
ans: Creating a distinct identity (name/logo/design) for a product (1) to differentiate it and build recognition/loyalty (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits of strong branding.
ans: Any two: recognition, loyalty/repeat purchase, premium pricing, easier launches (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two roles of packaging.
ans: Any two: protect the product, attract attention, inform, promote the brand, differentiate (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way packaging can be a USP.
ans: Distinctive/eco-friendly/reusable design that sets it apart (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘place’ (in the marketing mix).
ans: How and where the product reaches the customer (1) – the channels of distribution (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between digital and physical distribution.
ans: Physical: via wholesalers/retailers/stores (1); digital: online/e-commerce/downloads (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two channels of distribution a manufacturer could use.
ans: Any two: direct to consumer, via retailer, via wholesaler then retailer, via agent, online (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit to a manufacturer of selling directly online.
ans: Higher margins (no intermediary), customer data, brand control (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two factors a business considers when choosing a distribution channel.
ans: Any two: type of product, target market/buying habits, cost/margin, control, reach (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one use of the Boston Matrix.
ans: Analyse the product portfolio / decide where to invest or divest (1).

B8.title: Operations management (Syllabus 4)
B8.theme: Knowledge recall: the transformation process, efficiency/productivity/sustainability, production methods, inventory, JIT, capacity utilisation and outsourcing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the ‘transformational process’.
ans: Converting inputs (resources) into outputs (goods/services) (1) that have greater value (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by ‘inputs’ and ‘outputs’.
ans: Inputs: resources used (land, labour, capital) (1); outputs: the finished goods/services produced (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between efficiency and effectiveness.
ans: Efficiency: producing with least waste/cost (1); effectiveness: achieving the intended objective/meeting needs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘productivity’.
ans: Output per unit of input in a given time (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘sustainability’ in operations.
ans: Producing without harming the environment/future generations’ needs (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘labour productivity’.
ans: Output per worker (1) in a given period (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula for labour productivity.
ans: Total output / number of workers (2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between capital-intensive and labour-intensive operations.
ans: Capital-intensive: relies mainly on machinery/technology (1); labour-intensive: relies mainly on human effort (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit of capital-intensive production.
ans: Consistent quality, high output/low unit cost, works continuously (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one benefit of labour-intensive production.
ans: Flexible, suits bespoke/craft work, lower capital cost (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘job production’.
ans: Producing one-off/custom items individually (1) to a customer’s specific requirements (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘batch production’.
ans: Producing groups (batches) of identical products (1) that move through each stage together (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘flow production’.
ans: Continuous mass production of standardised products (1) on a production line (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘mass customisation’.
ans: Using flexible production (1) to make large volumes of individually tailored products at near mass-production cost (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one advantage of job production.
ans: Meets exact needs, premium price, high quality (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of flow production.
ans: Low unit cost at volume, consistent quality (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one problem of changing from batch to flow production.
ans: High investment, retraining, downtime, loss of flexibility (1).

parts.text: State the three types of inventory held by a manufacturer.
ans: Raw materials, work in progress, finished goods (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘buffer inventory’.
ans: A minimum level of stock held as a safety margin (1) to cover unexpected demand or delivery delays (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘lead time’.
ans: The time between placing an order and receiving the goods (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘re-order level’.
ans: The stock level at which a new order is placed (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two costs of holding inventory.
ans: Any two: storage, insurance, obsolescence/spoilage, cash tied up (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits of holding inventory.
ans: Any two: meets unexpected demand, avoids stock-outs, buffers delays, bulk discounts (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘Just in Time (JIT)’.
ans: An approach where materials arrive exactly when needed (1), minimising stock held (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘Just in Case (JIC)’.
ans: Holding buffer stock ‘just in case’ (1) to protect against demand/supply fluctuations (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one benefit of JIT.
ans: Lower holding costs, less cash tied up, less waste (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one risk of JIT.
ans: Vulnerable to supply disruption/stock-outs (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one requirement for JIT to work.
ans: Reliable suppliers, frequent deliveries, accurate forecasting (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘supply chain management’.
ans: Managing the flow of materials, goods and information (1) from suppliers through production to the customer (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit of effective supply chain management.
ans: Lower costs/lead times, reliable supply, better quality/service (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘capacity utilisation’.
ans: The percentage of maximum possible output (1) currently being used (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula for capacity utilisation.
ans: (Current output / maximum possible output) × 100 (2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one problem of operating at very low capacity utilisation.
ans: High fixed cost per unit, idle resources, low profit (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one problem of operating at (or above) full capacity for long.
ans: No slack for orders/maintenance, overworked staff/machines, quality falls (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way to improve low capacity utilisation.
ans: Increase demand (marketing), rationalise capacity, subcontract for others (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘rationalisation’.
ans: Reducing capacity/resources (1) to cut costs and raise efficiency/utilisation (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why higher capacity utilisation lowers unit costs.
ans: Fixed costs are spread over more units (1), reducing fixed cost per unit (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘outsourcing’.
ans: Contracting a business activity out to an external provider (1) rather than doing it in-house (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit of outsourcing.
ans: Lower cost, specialist expertise, flexibility, focus on core (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one drawback of outsourcing.
ans: Less control over quality/timing, reliance on supplier, reputation risk (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two measures that could improve the sustainability of operations.
ans: Any two: recycle/reduce waste, energy-efficient equipment, renewable energy, sustainable materials (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit to a business of more sustainable operations.
ans: Lower long-run costs, better reputation, meets regulation/customer demand (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one way to increase a business’s capacity.
ans: Invest in machinery/premises, hire staff, add shifts/overtime, outsource (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how productivity and unit costs are linked.
ans: Higher productivity lowers labour/variable cost per unit (1), reducing average cost (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how added value is created in operations.
ans: Efficient transformation of inputs into outputs (1) worth more than the input cost (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way to read an inventory control chart.
ans: Identify maximum, re-order and buffer levels (1) and when stock hits the re-order level (1).

B9.title: Business finance, sources & cash flow (Syllabus 5.1–5.3)
B9.theme: Knowledge recall: the need for finance, cash vs profit, working capital, internal & external sources of finance, and cash flow forecasts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons a business needs finance.
ans: Any two: to start up, fund day-to-day operations, grow/expand, survive a shortfall, buy assets (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between a short-term and long-term need for finance.
ans: Short-term: day-to-day/working capital (1); long-term: non-current assets/expansion (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between cash and profit.
ans: Profit: revenue minus expenses over a period (1); cash: actual money flowing in/out, with different timing (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason a profitable business can run out of cash.
ans: Cash tied up in receivables/inventory or spent on assets/loan repayments (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘insolvency’.
ans: Being unable to pay debts as they fall due (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘bankruptcy’.
ans: A legal status when an individual/business cannot repay its debts (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘liquidation’.
ans: Closing a company and selling its assets to repay creditors (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘administration’.
ans: A process where an administrator runs a struggling company (1) to try to rescue it or get a better result for creditors (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘working capital’.
ans: The finance available for day-to-day operations (1); current assets minus current liabilities (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the working capital formula.
ans: Working capital = current assets − current liabilities (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between trade receivables and trade payables.
ans: Receivables: money owed to the business by credit customers (1); payables: money the business owes suppliers (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way to reduce trade receivables.
ans: Tighter credit terms, prompt-payment discounts, debt factoring, credit checks (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between capital and revenue expenditure.
ans: Capital: spending on non-current assets used long-term (1); revenue: day-to-day running costs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of each.
ans: Capital: machinery/premises (1); revenue: wages/materials/rent (1).

parts.text: State four internal sources of finance.
ans: Any four: retained earnings, sale of unwanted assets, sale and leaseback, working capital, owner’s investment (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘retained earnings’.
ans: Profit kept in the business (1) rather than distributed to owners, used to fund activities (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of using retained earnings.
ans: No interest/repayment, no loss of control (1).

parts.text: State four external sources of finance.
ans: Any four: share capital, debentures, bank loan, overdraft, leasing, hire purchase, mortgage, debt factoring, trade credit, venture capital, crowdfunding, microfinance, government grant (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘share capital’.
ans: Finance raised by selling shares (1) to shareholders who become part-owners (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘debenture’.
ans: A long-term loan to a company (1) that pays fixed interest and is repaid on a set date (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a bank loan and a bank overdraft.
ans: Loan: fixed sum repaid with interest over a set period (long-term) (1); overdraft: withdraw more than the balance up to a limit (short-term) (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one situation where an overdraft is suitable.
ans: Covering a short-term/seasonal cash shortfall (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘leasing’.
ans: Paying to use an asset (1) without owning it, via regular payments (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘hire purchase’.
ans: Buying an asset by paying in instalments (1); ownership passes after the final payment (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘trade credit’.
ans: Buying goods/materials from suppliers now (1) and paying later (e.g. within 30–60 days) (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘debt factoring’.
ans: Selling trade receivables to a factor (1) for immediate cash (at a discount) (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘venture capital’.
ans: Finance from investors to high-risk, high-potential businesses (1), usually for an equity stake (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘crowdfunding’.
ans: Raising small amounts from many people (1), usually via an online platform (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘microfinance’.
ans: Small-scale financial services/loans (1) for people/businesses with limited access to normal banking (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘government grant’.
ans: Money given by government that usually does not need to be repaid (1).

parts.text: State four factors that affect the choice of a source of finance.
ans: Any four: cost, flexibility, need to retain control, use/purpose (short vs long term), level of existing debt, risk (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how the form of ownership affects finance available.
ans: Sole traders/partnerships cannot sell shares (limited sources) (1); companies (esp. plcs) can raise share capital (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one source of finance suitable for a sole trader.
ans: Owner’s savings, bank loan, overdraft, trade credit, microfinance (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘cash flow forecast’.
ans: An estimate of expected cash inflows and outflows (1) over a future period (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘net cash flow’.
ans: Cash inflows minus cash outflows in a period (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how to calculate the closing cash balance.
ans: Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the link between the closing balance and the next opening balance.
ans: The closing balance of one period is the opening balance of the next (1).

parts.text: State four ways a business could improve its cash flow.
ans: Any four: chase receivables/tighten credit, negotiate longer supplier credit, reduce inventory, cut costs, arrange an overdraft, delay capital spending, sale and leaseback (1 each).

B10.title: Costs, break-even, budgets & variances (Syllabus 5.4 & 5.5)
B10.theme: Knowledge recall: types of cost, full & contribution costing, break-even analysis, budgets and variances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘fixed costs’.
ans: Costs that do not change with output, e.g. rent (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘variable costs’.
ans: Costs that change directly with output, e.g. materials (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Distinguish between direct and indirect costs.
ans: Direct: attributable to a specific product/cost centre (1); indirect (overheads): cannot be directly attributed (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘total cost’.
ans: Fixed costs plus total variable costs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘average (unit) cost’.
ans: Total cost divided by output (1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define ‘marginal cost’.
ans: The cost of producing one extra unit of output (2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why accurate cost information is important.
ans: For pricing decisions (1) and to monitor/control performance and calculate profit (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one use of cost information.
ans: Pricing, budgeting, make-or-buy, special orders, profit calculation (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between full costing and contribution costing.
ans: Full (absorption): allocates all costs including overheads to each product (1); contribution: charges only variable costs, fixed costs treated as a period cost (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one limitation of full costing.
ans: Overhead allocation is often arbitrary, distorting product costs (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘contribution per unit’.
ans: Selling price per unit (1) minus variable cost per unit (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula for total contribution.
ans: Contribution per unit × quantity sold (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between contribution and profit.
ans: Contribution = sales minus variable costs (covers fixed costs first) (1); profit = total contribution minus fixed costs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one situation where contribution costing is useful.
ans: Special-order/make-or-buy decisions or break-even analysis (1) where fixed costs are already covered (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘break-even level of output’.
ans: The output at which total revenue equals total cost (1) – no profit or loss (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula for break-even output.
ans: Break-even = fixed costs / contribution per unit (2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘margin of safety’.
ans: The amount by which actual/current output exceeds the break-even output (1) – how far sales can fall before a loss (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the formula for margin of safety.
ans: Margin of safety = actual output − break-even output (1).

parts.text: A firm has fixed costs of $30,000, price $20 and variable cost $8. State the contribution per unit and the break-even output.
ans: =Contribution = 20 − 8 = $12 (2)
=Break-even = 30,000 / 12 = 2,500 units (2)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two uses of break-even analysis.
ans: Any two: set output/sales targets, assess price/cost changes, support finance applications, find margin of safety (1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two limitations of break-even analysis.
ans: Any two: assumes all output sold, constant price/costs, ignores discounts/economies of scale, only as good as the data (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the break-even point is on a break-even chart.
ans: Where the total revenue line crosses the total cost line (1) – output where TR = TC (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the area beyond break-even (up to current output) represents.
ans: Profit (and the margin of safety) (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how contribution helps a special-order decision.
ans: Accept if the price exceeds variable cost (positive contribution) (1), since fixed costs are already covered it adds to profit (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one situation where contribution costing should not be used for pricing.
ans: Long-term/all pricing – fixed costs must eventually be covered (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘budget’.
ans: A financial plan for a future period (1) setting out expected income and/or expenditure (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two purposes of budgeting.
ans: Any two: planning, control/monitoring, motivation, coordination, resource allocation (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘incremental budget’.
ans: A budget based on the previous period’s figures (1) adjusted by a set amount/percentage (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define ‘zero-based budget’.
ans: A budget where every item must be justified from zero each period (1) rather than based on the past (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘flexible budget’.
ans: A budget adjusted to reflect the actual level of activity/output (1) so costs are compared at the achieved output (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of zero-based budgeting.
ans: Avoids carrying forward waste, forces justification/efficiency (1).

parts.text: State four uses of budgets.
ans: Any four: planning, allocating resources, controlling/monitoring, measuring performance, motivating staff, coordination (1 each).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define ‘variance’.
ans: The difference between a budgeted figure and the actual figure (1) for income or costs (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Distinguish between a favourable and an adverse variance.
ans: Favourable: actual is better than budget (higher revenue/profit or lower cost) (1); adverse: actual is worse than budget (1).

parts.text: Budgeted cost was $50,000; actual cost was $57,000. State the variance and its type.
ans: =Variance = 57,000 − 50,000 = $7,000 higher cost (2)
$7,000 ADVERSE (1)

parts.text: Budgeted revenue was $120,000; actual revenue was $135,000. State the variance and its type.
ans: =Variance = 135,000 − 120,000 = $15,000 higher revenue (2)
$15,000 FAVOURABLE (1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one benefit of investigating variances.
ans: Identifies problems/successes early for corrective action (1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a favourable variance is not always good.
ans: It may reflect cut corners/quality or under-investment (1), or an unrealistic budget (1).
